O  R  D  E  R
Heard Mr. Ajit Kumar Sinha, learned  Amicus Curiae  (Senior
Advocate) and learned senior counsel/counsel for the parties.
2. Apropos issue(s) relating to the Bhopal Municipal Corporation,
we have been informed that upon survey, about 1,000 notices have

## Page 31

10
been issued and many places sealed pursuant thereto and further
that, consequential orders have also been passed. However, it was
brought to the notice of the Court by Mr. K.M. Nataraj, learned
Additional  Solicitor  General1,  representing  the  said  Municipal
Corporation that the Madhya Pradesh High Court at Jabalpur in
various cases has granted stay/interim relief, as people have
bypassed the statutory mechanism under the concerned statute and
directly approached the High Court.
3. Learned  Amicus  Curiae  submits  that  under  similar
circumstances, coordinate Benches have been constrained to direct
that consequences as per the Orders passed in those cases by this
Court should prevail irrespective of any order passed by the High
Court or the statutory forum. 
4. Having regard to the aforesaid position, we may be constrained
to pass similar Order(s). We would request learned Amicus Curiae to
compile a list of such Order(s) as passed by Coordinate Benches of
this Court, to enable us to examine what Order is called for on the
next date.
5.  For the present, we request the Madhya Pradesh High Court to
endeavour to decide the cases where it has granted stay/interim
relief, within six weeks hereafter.
6. At this juncture, our attention was drawn to the fact that
initially the Bhopal Municipal Corporation had sealed about 100
premises, but later, the seals were removed by the same authority.
7. On our query, Mr. Nataraj, learned ASG, drew the attention of
the Court to an administrative order issued by the Government of
1  ‘ASG’.

## Page 32

11
Madhya  Pradesh,  General  Administration  Department,  dated
02.08.2026, whereby a 10-Member Committee has been constituted,
purportedly, to come up with suggestions for procedural and policy
decision-making to ensure compliance of the Judgment in Rajendra
Kumar Barjatya v U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad, 2024 INSC 990 dated
17.12.2024, penned by one us (R. Mahadevan, J.) and our Order dated
20.05.2026 in the present proceeding. 
8. Learned counsel for the State of Madhya Pradesh submits that
the administrative order supra is clarificatory in nature, at best,
as the Government of Madhya Pradesh wishes to have a clear-cut
policy on the matter. 
9. We have no hesitation to hold that the said administrative
order is prima facie contemptuous and seems intended to interfere
with the administration of justice. Accordingly, the administrative
order shall be kept in abeyance with immediate effect. Original
file and records leading up to the constitution of this Committee
be placed before us on the next date. Formal notice of contempt to
the concerned may follow thereupon. Let this serve as a deterrent
for any further/similar attempt to interfere with the directions
issued by this Court.
10. Coming to the Patna Municipal Corporation, pursuant to our
earlier Order, a fresh affidavit has been filed bringing on record
the fact that after the survey conducted, as of now, a total of
26,746 cases have been found, where residential property has been
put to non-residential/commercial use. The figure itself leaves
nothing  to  doubt  that  there  has  been  total  abdication  of

## Page 33

12
responsibility on behalf of the concerned Municipal Commissioners.
The Patna Municipal Corporation was not even aware of such wide-
spread violation and the alleged violators, till the time this
Court took up the matter. We are informed that the present
incumbent has been on the post since October 2025 and prior
thereto, Mr. Animesh Kumar Parashar, I.A.S., was posted from
26.11.2021 to 04.10.2025 i.e., for close to four years.
11.   In the affidavit filed by Mr. Parashar, I.A.S., it is stated
that his tenure saw about 500 cases pertaining to violations of
municipal bye-laws, of which 81 cases were initiated suo motu and
orders were passed in 129 cases and besides these, more than 397
complaints and 22 miscellaneous cases were dealt with by him in
accordance with law.
12.  We find no justification in such figures for an officer who
held the post for almost four years. It, tentatively, shows that
the officer had no real concern with regard to what was transpiring
on the ground level.
13. In the aforesaid background, we put him to notice, as to why,
the Court may not pass appropriate orders against him for such
slackness shown during his term as Municipal Commissioner, Patna
Municipal Corporation. He shall be personally present before this
Court along with his Show-Cause on the next date.
14. We are also not satisfied with the action taken by the present
Municipal Commissioner, Patna Municipal Corporation inasmuch as the
notices have still not been served to a majority of the alleged
violators.

## Page 34

13
15. We are assured by Mr. S. D. Sanjay, learned Advocate General,
State of Bihar that latest within four weeks from date, notices
shall be served on all concerned. Let the same be positively done.
16. Compliance affidavits be filed by all concerned, latest within
four weeks from today. 
17. Though, on 04.08.2026 (Para 28), we had directed States/UTs
which had not deposited Rs.50,000/- (Rupees Fifty Thousand) to
deposit Rs.1,00,000/- (Rupees One Lakh) by today, as formally they
have  been  made  parties  only  yesterday,  the  time  to  deposit
Rs.50,000/- (Rupees Fifty Thousand) stands extended till next
Tuesday i.e., 11.08.2026. Needful be done by that date. Apropos
other States, where the concerned Municipal Corporations or other
statutory bodies have deposited monies on behalf of the concerned
State/UT, they shall be reimbursed by the concerned State/UT. Same
indulgence  is  extended  to  all  who  deposit  the  amounts  by
11.08.2026.
18. The amounts lying with the Registry be deposited in an
interest-bearing fixed deposit initially for a period of three
months with auto-renewal facility.
19. The direction for carrying out a physical survey of specified
areas  under  the  New  Delhi  Municipal  Council 2 and  Municipal
Corporation of Delhi3, the exercise has not been completed. Though
we are thoroughly dissatisfied with the manner in which the
concerned parties have coordinated amongst themselves, we refrain
from passing coercive orders,  in praesenti . Accordingly, and as
2  ‘NDMC’.
3  ‘MCD’.

## Page 35

14
informed by the learned counsel for IIT-Delhi that two Professors
have been deputed for the exercise and now only draftsmen remain to
be nominated, we substitute our earlier direction. Let NDMC and MCD
provide two competent draftsmen each for the purpose. Exercise be
carried out in terms of Order dated 09.07.2026, at any rate within
three weeks from today, without fail. 
20. The survey in Lucknow be also completed within a period of
three weeks from today.
21. Reports be submitted to the learned Amicus Curiae.
22. In terms of yesterday’s order, Mr. Prathmesh Kumar, presently
Vice-Chairman, Lucknow Development Authority, is present in the
Court and has filed an affidavit. Apology has been tendered. Though
the same is not in the form of a reply to the Show-Cause, he has
indicated the steps undertaken as also action taken against the
officers involved in/responsible for blatant violation of municipal
laws.
23. It has been submitted that 51 properties have been identified
and  action  initiated,  which  would  be  taken  to  its  logical
conclusion without delay. It was further submitted that follow-up
exercise would continue in the entire jurisdictional span of the
Lucknow Development Authority on a war-footing. 
24. Let the same be completed within three weeks. The State of
Uttar Pradesh is also directed to ensure that the proceedings
started are taken up seriously and conducted expeditiously, without
any slackness or favouritism or indulgence being shown to the
delinquent  officers  concerned.  The  Vice-Chairman,  Lucknow

## Page 36

Development Authority, has assured that the Presenting Officer(s)
would be a person(s) of impeccable integrity competent to handle
the said.
25. Mr. Nataraj, learned ASG, assured that the Court would not

bona fide.
26. Having regard to the aforesaid, we accept the apology tendered
by the Vice-Chairman, Lucknow Development Authority. Issue relating
to contempt stands closed. His personal appearance also stands

Heard Mr. Ajit Kumar Sinha, learned  Amicus Curiae  (Senior
Advocate) and learned senior counsel/counsel for the parties.
2. Apropos issue(s) relating to the Bhopal Municipal Corporation,
we have been informed that upon survey, about 1,000 notices have

## Page 46

25
been issued and many places sealed pursuant thereto and further
that, consequential orders have also been passed. However, it was
brought to the notice of the Court by Mr. K.M. Nataraj, learned
Additional  Solicitor  General4,  representing  the  said  Municipal
Corporation that the Madhya Pradesh High Court at Jabalpur in
various cases has granted stay/interim relief, as people have
bypassed the statutory mechanism under the concerned statute and
directly approached the High Court.
3. Learned  Amicus  Curiae  submits  that  under  similar
circumstances, coordinate Benches have been constrained to direct
that consequences as per the Orders passed in those cases by this
Court should prevail irrespective of any order passed by the High
Court or the statutory forum. 
4. Having regard to the aforesaid position, we may be constrained
to pass similar Order(s). We would request learned Amicus Curiae to
compile a list of such Order(s) as passed by Coordinate Benches of
this Court, to enable us to examine what Order is called for on the
next date.
5.  For the present, we request the Madhya Pradesh High Court to
endeavour to decide the cases where it has granted stay/interim
relief, within six weeks hereafter.
6. At this juncture, our attention was drawn to the fact that
initially the Bhopal Municipal Corporation had sealed about 100
premises, but later, the seals were removed by the same authority.
7. On our query, Mr. Nataraj, learned ASG, drew the attention of
the Court to an administrative order issued by the Government of
4  ‘ASG’.

## Page 47

26
Madhya  Pradesh,  General  Administration  Department,  dated
02.08.2026, whereby a 10-Member Committee has been constituted,
purportedly, to come up with suggestions for procedural and policy
decision-making to ensure compliance of the Judgment in Rajendra
Kumar Barjatya v U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad, 2024 INSC 990 dated
17.12.2024, penned by one us (R. Mahadevan, J.) and our Order dated
20.05.2026 in the present proceeding. 
8. Learned counsel for the State of Madhya Pradesh submits that
the administrative order supra is clarificatory in nature, at best,
as the Government of Madhya Pradesh wishes to have a clear-cut
policy on the matter. 
9. We have no hesitation to hold that the said administrative
order is prima facie contemptuous and seems intended to interfere
with the administration of justice. Accordingly, the administrative
order shall be kept in abeyance with immediate effect. Original
file and records leading up to the constitution of this Committee
be placed before us on the next date. Formal notice of contempt to
the concerned may follow thereupon. Let this serve as a deterrent
for any further/similar attempt to interfere with the directions
issued by this Court.
10. Coming to the Patna Municipal Corporation, pursuant to our
earlier Order, a fresh affidavit has been filed bringing on record
the fact that after the survey conducted, as of now, a total of
26,746 cases have been found, where residential property has been
put to non-residential/commercial use. The figure itself leaves
nothing  to  doubt  that  there  has  been  total  abdication  of

## Page 48

27
responsibility on behalf of the concerned Municipal Commissioners.
The Patna Municipal Corporation was not even aware of such wide-
spread violation and the alleged violators, till the time this
Court took up the matter. We are informed that the present
incumbent has been on the post since October 2025 and prior
thereto, Mr. Animesh Kumar Parashar, I.A.S., was posted from
26.11.2021 to 04.10.2025 i.e., for close to four years.
11.   In the affidavit filed by Mr. Parashar, I.A.S., it is stated
that his tenure saw about 500 cases pertaining to violations of
municipal bye-laws, of which 81 cases were initiated suo motu and
orders were passed in 129 cases and besides these, more than 397
complaints and 22 miscellaneous cases were dealt with by him in
accordance with law.
12.  We find no justification in such figures for an officer who
held the post for almost four years. It, tentatively, shows that
the officer had no real concern with regard to what was transpiring
on the ground level.
13. In the aforesaid background, we put him to notice, as to why,
the Court may not pass appropriate orders against him for such
slackness shown during his term as Municipal Commissioner, Patna
Municipal Corporation. He shall be personally present before this
Court along with his Show-Cause on the next date.
14. We are also not satisfied with the action taken by the present
Municipal Commissioner, Patna Municipal Corporation inasmuch as the
notices have still not been served to a majority of the alleged
violators.

## Page 49

28
15. We are assured by Mr. S. D. Sanjay, learned Advocate General,
State of Bihar that latest within four weeks from date, notices
shall be served on all concerned. Let the same be positively done.
16. Compliance affidavits be filed by all concerned, latest within
four weeks from today. 
17. Though, on 04.08.2026 (Para 28), we had directed States/UTs
which had not deposited Rs.50,000/- (Rupees Fifty Thousand) to
deposit Rs.1,00,000/- (Rupees One Lakh) by today, as formally they
have  been  made  parties  only  yesterday,  the  time  to  deposit
Rs.50,000/- (Rupees Fifty Thousand) stands extended till next
Tuesday i.e., 11.08.2026. Needful be done by that date. Apropos
other States, where the concerned Municipal Corporations or other
statutory bodies have deposited monies on behalf of the concerned
State/UT, they shall be reimbursed by the concerned State/UT. Same
indulgence  is  extended  to  all  who  deposit  the  amounts  by
11.08.2026.
18. The amounts lying with the Registry be deposited in an
interest-bearing fixed deposit initially for a period of three
months with auto-renewal facility.
19. The direction for carrying out a physical survey of specified
areas  under  the  New  Delhi  Municipal  Council 5 and  Municipal
Corporation of Delhi6, the exercise has not been completed. Though
we are thoroughly dissatisfied with the manner in which the
concerned parties have coordinated amongst themselves, we refrain
from passing coercive orders,  in praesenti . Accordingly, and as
5  ‘NDMC’.
6  ‘MCD’.

29
informed by the learned counsel for IIT-Delhi that two Professors
have been deputed for the exercise and now only draftsmen remain to
be nominated, we substitute our earlier direction. Let NDMC and MCD
provide two competent draftsmen each for the purpose. Exercise be
carried out in terms of Order dated 09.07.2026, at any rate within
three weeks from today, without fail. 
20. The survey in Lucknow be also completed within a period of
three weeks from today.
21. Reports be submitted to the learned Amicus Curiae.
22. In terms of yesterday’s order, Mr. Prathmesh Kumar, presently
Vice-Chairman, Lucknow Development Authority, is present in the
Court and has filed an affidavit. Apology has been tendered. Though
the same is not in the form of a reply to the Show-Cause, he has
indicated the steps undertaken as also action taken against the
officers involved in/responsible for blatant violation of municipal
laws.
23. It has been submitted that 51 properties have been identified
and  action  initiated,  which  would  be  taken  to  its  logical
conclusion without delay. It was further submitted that follow-up
exercise would continue in the entire jurisdictional span of the
Lucknow Development Authority on a war-footing. 
24. Let the same be completed within three weeks. The State of
Uttar Pradesh is also directed to ensure that the proceedings
started are taken up seriously and conducted expeditiously, without
any slackness or favouritism or indulgence being shown to the
delinquent  officers  concerned.  The  Vice-Chairman,  Lucknow

## Page 51

Development Authority, has assured that the Presenting Officer(s)
would be a person(s) of impeccable integrity competent to handle
the said.
25. Mr. Nataraj, learned ASG, assured that the Court would not

bona fide.
26. Having regard to the aforesaid, we accept the apology tendered
by the Vice-Chairman, Lucknow Development Authority. Issue relating
to contempt stands closed. His personal appearance also stands
dispensed with, for the present.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. This Court is presently seized of the matter pertaining to the
rival claims of the parents in seeking custody of their child, who
is about four years and one month old (born on 15.07.2022).
2. Admittedly, the mother and father are not married to each
other. The relationship between the parties commenced sometime in
January 2019 in the course of their professional interactions.
Subsequently, a child was born on 15.07.2022 at La Femme, Hospital,
New Delhi, India. The mother is a German citizen employed as a Vice
President of Public Policy at TikTok, based in Singapore. The
father is admittedly a practicing lawyer, and  partner of a law
firm, PLR Chambers, based in Delhi.
3. This Court is considering the rival claims of the parties  for
custody of their child. We have interacted with the mother and
father in person on several occasions and have also observed the
behavior of the child. Though certain allegations and counter-
allegations have been made by the parties against each other, the
child does not appear to have any aversion towards either of the
parents. Both parents also appear to be doting parents. The child
is presently in Indi a. For varying periods of time, the child has
stayed with the parents in India, including in Delhi and Goa, and
has recently stayed with the father in Kolkata, which according to
the mother was without her consent. The child has also travelled to
and stayed in Singapore on a couple of occasions, along with his
parents, and has travelled to and stayed in Germany with the family
PETITION FOR SPECIAL LEAVE TO APPEAL (CRL.)  NO.11625/2026

## Page 110

3
of the mother.
4. The mother initiated writ proceedings before the High Court of
Bombay at Goa Bench, in February 2026, seeking access to the child,
as she claims to have been denied access to the child by the father
without any reason. The matter is pending before the High Court of
Bombay at Goa Bench out of which the present proceeding has arisen
before this Court . The High Court initially granted the mother
access to the child for 10 days, and thereafter passed certain
orders for continued access to the child, the details of which may
not be necessary to be referred to herein. After the filing of the
writ proceedings before the High Court of Bombay at Goa, the father
filed a petition under the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 in the
Court of the District Judge, South 24-Parganas at Alipore in April
2026, seeking protection and custody of the child. In the writ
petition filed by the mother, she also sought custody of the child
and permission to take the child to Singapore. The mother is keen
to provide education to the child in Singapore, where she lived for
the last several years. The child’s admission to one of the best
schools in Singapore is stated to be under process, where the
mother would also be able to provide quality time to the child in
Singapore. The father, on the other hand, seeks to retain custody
of the child in India, which he claims to be the child's habitual
residence  and  will  be  in  the  child's  welfare where  quality
education can be provided.
5. In considering such rival claims and counter-claims, this
Court has to keep the best interests of the child as the foremost
PETITION FOR SPECIAL LEAVE TO APPEAL (CRL.)  NO.11625/2026

## Page 111

4
consideration, apart from the claim of the biological mother based
on maternal love, affection and maternal instincts, as well as that
of the father. In our view, this would obviously necessitate an
evaluation of the various physical and mental conditions of all
concerned, including the child , as neither have agreed to joint
custody so far.
6.  The father is primarily based in India because of his legal
profession, while the mother is primarily based in Singapore
because of her professional commitments. Therefore, if the child is
to remain in India with the father, the mother will not have access
to the child for a substantial period of time, except  during
occasional visits to India. Similarly, if the child is placed in
Singapore as desired by the mother, the father will not be in a
position to spend substantial time with the child, except during
occasional visits. Under such circumstances, accepting the request
of either parent would necessarily entail dislocation of the other
parent for a substantial period of time. In abse nce of any
agreement between the parties, the child has to remain either in
India or in Singapore.
7. Under the circumstances, this Court has felt the necessity to
seek  the  views  of  experts,  particularly  child
psychologists/behavioural specialists, who may interact with the
child as well as with the parents, either separately or together,
as the psychologists/experts may deem fit and appropriate, and
apprise this Court of their views. Thereafter, this Court will be
in a better position to understand the psychological impact on the
PETITION FOR SPECIAL LEAVE TO APPEAL (CRL.)  NO.11625/2026

## Page 112

5
child if either parent is unable to remain with the child for a
prolonged period of time, and thereafter to determine the issue of
custody of the child.
     Therefore, this Court would like to ascertain the comparative
psychological impact on the child of the two possible arrangements,
namely, the child continuing to reside in India with the father in
the absence of the mother for substantial period, or the child
residing in Singapore with the mother in the absence of the father
for substantial period, and which of these two arrangements would
better serve the welfare and best interests of the child. The
experts may accordingly examine the comparative merits, demerits
and implications of both alternatives and place their considered
opinion before this Court, keeping in mind that the child is only
about 4 years old, the psychological harm it may cause if the child
is deprived of the maternal love and affection for a prolonged
period, as compared to deprivation of the love and affection of his
father.
In either eventuality, the parent with whom the child does not
ordinarily reside shall have reasonable and meaningful access to
the child, including regular interaction through video conferencing
and  appropriate  weekly/monthly  visitation  rights,  as  may  be
feasible and conducive to the best interests of the child.
8. From the records, we have also seen that the child has been
looked after by nannies named, Kusum and Anu, for a substantial
period of time. If the experts so desire, they may examine them
also, as they may provide valuable insights into the behaviour,
PETITION FOR SPECIAL LEAVE TO APPEAL (CRL.)  NO.11625/2026

## Page 113

6
predisposition of the child and the role of the parents.
9.   The experts may also give their views as to whether they need
to visit any particular place, either in India or in Singapore, as
the case may be, to ascertain the proposed physical environment of
the child whe re the child may be placed for the time being , for
which the parties shall  make the necessary arrangements for travel
and stay and both the parties will share the expenses.
10.  For the aforesaid purpose, we request the National institute
of mental health and Neuro Sciences (hereinafter ‘NIMHANS’) at
Bengaluru to immediately constitute a panel of experts consisting
of such members as they  may deem fit and appropriate  who shall
examine the child and parents,  considering the aforementioned
background and desire of the parents, keeping in mind the best
interests of the child.
11.  Considering the nature of the case and also the limitations on
the mother to physically remain in India beyond a limited period,
which have been appreciated by all, including the father, we would
request  the  NIMHANS  authorities  to  initiate  the  process  of
interaction without any further delay.
12.  The parties have agreed to visit NIMHANS, Bengaluru, with the
child immediately and shall report to NIMHANS at such time and
place as may be required. If the NIMHANS authorities feel that it
would be better for the parties to stay in their complex for some
time,  the  parties  shall  cooperate  and  stay  in  the  complex.
Otherwise, they may stay at a hotel near NIMHANS, as per their
convenience.
PETITION FOR SPECIAL LEAVE TO APPEAL (CRL.)  NO.11625/2026

## Page 114

7
13.  The mother has expressed that her child is very proficient in
German language and that she would like to interact with the child
in German during the interaction, and the experts may also interact
with the child in German with the help of an expert/ interpreter.
14. Considering the nature of the case, we have requested Ms.
Aishwarya Bhati, learned ASG, to assist the Court for expediting
the constitution of the Board of experts by NIMHANS and also to
render necessary assistance in requesting the services of a German-
speaking person fluent in English, preferably a German national
based in Bengaluru to assist the Board of Experts and also the
mother and child. 
15.  NIMHANS is requested to submit a report  before this Court in
a sealed cover , preferably within a period of 2–3 weeks, from
today. However, if the NIMHANS authorities feel the need for
extension of time for this exercise, they may do so, which may be
communicated  to the learned ASG,  Ms. Aishwarya Bhati, who will
apprise this Court of such requirement . NIMHANS shall accordingly
inform both parties through email as well as text messages on their
mobile  phones  and  shall  also  inform  their  respective
lawyers/counsels regarding the date and time of their presence
required at NIMHANS, Bengaluru.
16.  This Court, for obvious reasons, is not going to make any
observation at this stage regarding the claims and counter-claims
or allegations/counter-allegations of the parties. However, to
apprise the Board of Experts, of the background of the case, the
PETITION FOR SPECIAL LEAVE TO APPEAL (CRL.)  NO.11625/2026

## Page 115

8
parties are at liberty to submit, in writing, their respective
cases,  with a short synopsis/list of dates, before the Medical
Board of NIMHANS within two days from today. The same shall not
exceed three pages /2000 words. Further, the parties shall also
submit their updated concrete plan/ proposals regarding the custody
and care of the child to the Board of Experts also, which was
earlier directed to be submitted before this Court.
17.  During this period, the interim custody of the child shall
remain with the mother during her stay in India. Obviously, the
father will also have access to the child at such convenient time
and place, as may be agreed between the parents. The  respective
counsel of the parties may help in this regard to the parties. It
goes without saying that, in the absence of the mother in India,
the interim custody of the child will revert back to the father,
till the mother returns to India who shall then take custody of the
child again from the father until such order of the Court.
18.  Regarding the pending guardianship petition bearing ‘Act VIII
Case No. 69 of 2026 (R-69)’,  before the Court of the District
Judge, South 24-Parganas at Alipore, it has been agreed by the both
parties that the same can conveniently be transferred to an
appropriate Court in Delhi. The Chief Justice of the High Court of
Delhi is requested to assign the matter to a specific Court in
Delhi at the earliest. The concerned Court at Alipore is directed
to send the records immediately to the High Court of Delhi, which
is to be sent to the appropriate Court in Delhi as per the
PETITION FOR SPECIAL LEAVE TO APPEAL (CRL.)  NO.11625/2026

## Page 116

9
directions of the Chief Justice of the High Court of Delhi.
19.  The costs of the entire exercise involved in the assessment
to be conducted by NIMHANS shall be borne by both parents equally,
for which each parent shall deposit a sum of Rs.2 lakhs with the
Registry of this Court within a period of 2 days. The expenses
incurred by NIMHANS towards payment of fees to counsellors, experts
and other ancillary expenditures shall be reimbursed from the
amounts so deposited by the parties in this regard. Any additional
amount, so required, shall be borne by the parties by depositing
the same with the Registry of this Court , as may be intimated to
the Registry by the NIMHANS.
20.  The passport of the petitioner, Helena Anna Maria Lersch , may
be returned to her so as to enable her to make the necessary
arrangements for her travel in India and  abroad, without any
restrictions. However, the passport of the child shall remain with
the Registry of this Court. The interim direction issued by this
Court restraining the removal of the child from the country without
the leave of the Court and other incidental directions issued
earlier shall also remain in force, subject to what has been
ordered today.
21.  A copy of this order be furnished to Ms. Aishwarya Bhati,
learned ASG, with a request that the authorities at NIMHANS be duly
intimated and also for engagement of an interpreter.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CONTEMPT PETITION NO.261/2026
IN CIVIL APPEAL No.10737 OF 2013
ANAND ANEGUNDI ..... APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
PRASHANT GOYAL ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. Leave granted.
3. We have heard Ms. Liz Mathew, learned senior counsel
for the appellant and Mr. Mayank Kshirsagar, learned counsel
for the respondent.
4. Appellant takes exception to the Order dated 30.09.2020,
passed by the High Court of Karnataka, Dharwad Bench (briefly
the ‘High Court’ hereinafter) allowing the Civil Revision
Petition filed by the respondent.
5. There was an arbitral proceeding between the parties.
While the learned Arbitrator has allowed the claim of the
respondent vide the award dated 12.06.2014, the counter claim
filed by the appellant was rejected.

## Page 129

6. Appellant filed an application under Section 33(4) of
the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (briefly the 1996
‘Act’ hereinafter) seeking correction in the award in as much
as  his  counter  claim  was  not  allowed  by  the  learned
Arbitrator.  By  the  Order  dated  16.08.2014,  the  learned
Arbitrator rejected the said application by holding that there
is no ground to pass any additional award under Section 33(4)
of the 1996 Act. 
7. After the Order dated 16.08.2014 was passed, appellant
filed an application under Section 34 of the 1996 Act before
the  Principal  District  and  Sessions  Judge,  Dharwad,  on
13.11.2014. Respondent  filed  Interlocutory  Application
No.21/2018 before the Section 34 Court contending that the said
application was barred by limitation. However, by the order dated
20.12.2018, the said Interlocutory Application was rejected
holding that the application filed under Section 34 was within
time and maintainable. 
8. It was this order which was challenged by the respondent
before  the  High  Court  in  Civil  Revision  Petition  No.
100014/2019. By the impugned order dated 30.09.2020, the High
Court allowed the Civil Revision Petition and set aside the
order of the District Court dated 20.12.2018. Consequently, the
Section 34 application came to be dismissed on the ground of
limitation. 
9. Learned senior counsel for the appellants submits that
2

## Page 130

issue raised in this appeal is no longer  res  integra . A
coordinate Bench of this Court in National Highway Authority
of India vs. T Younis,  2026 SCC OnLine SC 1060, has held that
once proceedings under Section 33 are initiated and entertained
by the Arbitral Tribunal, the award remained subject to the
limited jurisdiction of the Arbitral Tribunal for correction
etc. Therefore, the limitation prescribed under Section 34(3)
can start only from the date on which the proceedings under
Section 33 are concluded.
10. Per contra Mr. Kshirsagar, learned counsel for the
respondent submits that the aforesaid judgment of this Court
is distinguishable on the facts of this case. In the instant
case, it was a frivolous application filed by the appellant
before the Arbitral Tribunal. Section 33 clearly provides for
the limited scope within the contours of which correction etc.
of arbitral award can be sought for. Appellant could not have
sought for an Additional Award in the guise of an application
under Section 33(4); the appellant actually sought for review
of the award which is not permissible. Therefore, the appeal
may be dismissed. 
11. Submissions made by learned counsel for the parties
have received the due consideration of this Court. 
12. Facts  are  not  in  dispute.  However,  for  a  proper
perspective, we may, at the outset, advert to Section 33 of
the 1996 Act which provides for correction and interpretation
3

## Page 131

of award and additional award. Section 33 reads thus:
33. Correction and interpretation of award;
additional award.—(1) Within thirty days from
the receipt of the arbitral award, unless
another period of time has been agreed upon by
the parties—
(a) a party, with notice to the other party,
may request the arbitral tribunal to correct
any  computation  errors,  any  clerical  or
typographical errors or any other errors of a
similar nature occurring in the award;
(b) if so agreed by the parties, a party, with
notice to the other party, may request the
arbitral tribunal to give an interpretation of
a specific point or part of the award.
(2) If the arbitral tribunal considers the
request  made  under  sub-section  (1)  to  be
justified, it shall make the correction or
give the interpretation within thirty days
from  the  receipt  of  the  request  and  the
interpretation shall form part of the arbitral
award.
(3) The arbitral tribunal may correct any
error of the type referred to in clause (a) of
sub-section (1), on its own initiative, within
thirty days from the date of the arbitral
award.
(4) Unless otherwise agreed by the parties, a
party with notice to the other party, may
request, within thirty days from the receipt
of the arbitral award, the arbitral tribunal
4

## Page 132

to make an additional arbitral award as to
claims presented in the arbitral proceedings
but omitted from the arbitral award.
(5) If the arbitral tribunal considers the
request  made  under  sub-section  (4)  to  be
justified,  it  shall  make  the  additional
arbitral award within sixty days from the
receipt of such request.
(6)  The  arbitral  tribunal  may  extend,  if
necessary, the period of time within which it
shall  make  a  correction,  give  an
interpretation or make an additional arbitral
award under sub-section (2) or sub-section
(5).
(7) Section 31 shall apply to a correction or
interpretation of the arbitral award or to an
additional  arbitral  award  made  under  this
section.
12.1.   An analysis of Section 33 would show that it speaks of
two conditions for which the jurisdiction under Section 33 can
be invoked. Firstly, a party to the arbitration proceedings may
request  the  Arbitral  Tribunal  to  correct  any  computation
errors, any clerical or typographical errors or any other
errors of a similar nature occurring in the award.  The second
condition is that a party with the agreement of the other
party and with notice to it, may request the Arbitral Tribunal
to give an interpretation of a specific point or part of the
award. The Arbitral Tribunal is also vested with  suo  moto
power to correct any error of the type contemplated as per the
5

## Page 133

first condition. In exercise of the aforesaid powers, an
Arbitral Tribunal has the power to make an additional award.
Ordinarily, the limitation for invoking the jurisdiction of
the Arbitral Tribunal under Section 33 is 30 days, unless
another period of time is agreed upon by the parties.
13. This brings us to Section 34 of the 1996 award which
provides for filing of an application for setting aside an
arbitral award. For the present case, sub-section (3) of
Section 34 is relevant and the same is extracted hereunder:
(3) An application for setting aside may not
be made after three months have elapsed from
the  date  on  which  the  party  making  that
application had received the arbitral award
or, if a request had been made under Section
33, from the date on which that request had
been disposed of by the arbitral tribunal:
Provided that if the Court is satisfied that
the  applicant  was  prevented  by  sufficient
cause from making the application within the
said period of three months it may entertain
the application within a further period of
thirty days, but not thereafter.
13.1.   As per this provision, an application for setting
aside an arbitral award is required to be made within three
months  from  the  date  on  which  the  party  making  that
application had received the arbitral award or if a request
has been made under Section 33 of the 1996 Act from the date
6

## Page 134

on which the request has been disposed of by the Arbitral
Tribunal. As per the proviso, if the Section 34 court is
satisfied that the applicant was prevented by sufficient cause
from making the application within the prescribed period of 03
months, it may entertain the application within a further
period of 30 days but not thereafter. What is relevant for the
present discourse is the main sub-section (3) itself. Though
the limitation for filing an application under Section 34 is
three months from the date of the receipt of a copy of the
arbitral award, the same is however subject to Section 33 if a
request has been made under that provision. 
14. Insofar the  present case is concerned, the arbitral
award is dated 12.06.2014. Appellant had sought correction in
the award under Section 33 (4) of the 1996 Act which was
rejected  by  the  order  of  the  learned  Arbitrator  dated
16.08.2014.  It  was  thereafter  that  appellant  filed  the
application under Section 34 of the 1996 Act on 13.11.2014.
Therefore, the application under Section 34 was filed within a
period of 03 months from the date on which the Section 33 (4)
application was disposed of by the learned Arbitrator. 
15. In T. Younis, this Court after adverting to Sections 33
and 34(3) of the 1996 Act held as follows:
14. Once proceedings under Section 33 are
initiated  and  entertained  by  the  Arbitral
Tribunal, the award remains subject to the
limited  jurisdiction  of  the  tribunal  for
7

## Page 135

correction, interpretation, or supplementation
as contemplated under the provision. So long
as  such  proceedings  remain  pending,  the
parties  cannot  be  compelled  to  institute
proceedings  under  Section  34  merely  as  a
matter of abundant caution. The parties can
effectively pursue their remedy under Section
34 only upon conclusion of the proceedings
under Section 33. Consequently, the limitation
prescribed under Section 34(3) can start only
from the date on which the proceedings under
Section 33 are disposed of. 
15.  In  our  view,  the  contention  of  the
Respondent that only an application which is
"maintainable" under Section 33 can defer the
commencement of limitation under Section 34(3),
cannot be accepted. Whether the application
under Section 33 ultimately succeeds or fails,
or whether the Arbitral Tribunal eventually
finds that no correction or modification of the
award is warranted, is not determinative for the
purpose of Section 34(3). What is relevant is
that whether the jurisdiction of the Arbitral
Tribunal under Section 33 had been formally
invoked  and  that  such  proceedings  remained
pending consideration before the tribunal.
16. We have gone through the order passed by the Arbitral
Tribunal on 16.08.2014 rejecting the application filed by the
appellant under Section 33(4) of the 1996 Act. On going
through the same, it cannot be said that any view was taken by
the Arbitral Tribunal that the said application was frivolous.
We also do not think so. The Section 34 Court was right in
8

## Page 136

holding that the application filed under that provision is
within time. In our considered opinion, the decision in T.
Younis is squarely applicable to the facts of the present
case.
17. Accordingly, impugned order dated 30.09.2020 passed by
the High Court is hereby set aside.
18. The appeal is thus allowed.
19. Consequently, the Section 34 application filed by the
appellant being Arbitration Suit No.5 of 2014 pending in the
Court of Principal District and Sessions Judge, Dharwad, shall
be heard and decided on its own merit in terms of the
provisions of the 1996 Act.
20. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL No. 5636 of 2024
PATELIYA DILIP KUMAR BHIMJI BHAI        APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
   UNION OF INDIA & ORS.       RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. We have heard Mr. A Velan, learned counsel for  
the appellant and Ms. Aishwariya Bhati, learned Addl.  
Solicitor General for the respondent(s).
2. Appellant takes exception to the order dated  
16.01.2023  passed  by  the  Armed  Forces  Tribunal,  
Regional  Bench,  Mumbai  (briefly  ‘the  Tribunal’  
hereinafter), rejecting the original application of  
the appellant.
3. It is stated that appellant joined the army on  
07.05.2001 and served as a Gunner in the 222 Medium  
Regiment. He was dismissed from service following a  
Summary Court Martial proceeding dated 05.08.2014.
4. The  charge  against  the  appellant  is  of  

## Page 149

overstaying leave by 231 days. He was granted leave  
from 10.08.2006 to 16.08.2006. When he failed to  
rejoin duties after expiry of the period of leave, he  
was  declared  as  a  deserter  on  17.08.2006.  Long  
thereafter,  231  days  to  be  precise,  appellant  
reported to the Unit on 05.04.2007.
5. A Summary Court Martial was ordered.
6. Having regard to the previous conduct of the  
appellant in overstaying leave on four occasions and  
there being no material on record to justify such  
overstay of leave, the penalty of dismissal was  
awarded.
7. This came to be challenged by the appellant  
before the Tribunal in Original Application No.52 of  
2012. By the judgment and order dated 13.01.2014, the  
Tribunal took the view that the sentence of dismissal  
was too harsh and not warranted in the facts of the  
case. The Tribunal, vide the judgment and order dated 
13.01.2014, remanded the matter back to the concerned  
authority to consider the mitigating circumstances and, 
if necessary, to give opportunity to the appellant to  
prove those circumstances. Interestingly, the Tribunal, 
2

## Page 150

while  remanding  the  matter  back,  confirmed  and  
maintained  the  order  of  conviction  passed  by  the 
Summary Court Martial.
8. On remand, the Summary Court Martial on 05.08.  
2014, after providing opportunity to the appellant  
and  considering  his  submissions,  reiterated  the  
punishment of dismissal from service. It may be  
mentioned that appellant did not produce any evidence  
in support of his written statement. He also could  
not produce any evidence to justify the overstay of  
leave and that he had informed anybody in the Unit  
about not being able to join duty on time or the  
circumstances warranting such overstay of leave.
9. Considering similar overstay of leave in the past  
and  the  punishments  which  were  imposed  on  the  
appellant, the Summary Court Martial reiterated the  
punishment  of  dismissal  vide the  proceeding  dated 
05.08.2014.
10. This came to be challenged before the Tribunal by  
the appellant in Original Application No.84 of 2017  
and  by  the  impugned  judgment  and  order  dated  
16.01.2023, the same came to be dismissed.
3

## Page 151

11. Learned counsel for the appellant has referred to  
Section 116 of the Army Act, 1950 and submits that  
constitution of the Summary Court Martial and holding  
of proceedings by it was not justified. Summary Court  
Martial can only be resorted to in an emergent  
situation, not in a situation such as this. He has  
also pointed out the gap between the two Summary  
Court Martial(s), the first one being on 25.04.2007  
and the second being on 05.08.2014. His contention is  
that in any view of the matter, the Second Summary  
Court Martial was not warranted.
12. On  the  other  hand,  learned  Addl.  Solicitor  
General submits that appellant was already granted a  
long rope by the authorities. In spite of several  
opportunities,  he  could  not  redeem  himself  and  
continued to commit similar offences for which he was  
rightly imposed the penalty of dismissal from service  
in terms of Section 39(b) of the Army Act, 1950. In a  
disciplined force like the army, such indiscipline  
cannot be tolerated. Any leniency shown would lead to  
breakdown  of  discipline.  Insofar  Summary  Court  
Martial proceedings are concerned, she submits that  
present one is a case before the cut-off date of  
4

## Page 152

05.07.2016 as per the judgment passed in  Randhir 
Singh versus Union of India [(2020) 14 Supreme Court  
Cases 513].
13. Submissions  made  by  learned  counsel  for  the  
parties have received the due consideration of the  
Court.
14. The Tribunal had carefully gone into the rival  
contentions and thereafter held as follows:
“13] There appears to be substance in the 
submission of respondent that applicant did 
not avail of the opportunity to submit  
evidence either documentary or in terms of 
witness to substantiate his case in the second 
Summary Court Martial. He did not even contact 
any person from his unit which also shows his 
basic callous attitude and indifference to his 
duties. Even prior to the long period of 
absence of 231 days, applicant had already 
been punished with rigorous imprisonment for 
committing similar type of misconduct of 
overstayal of leave without sufficient cause. 
Thus, the applicant showed scant respect of 
observing discipline in the institution where 
observance  of  appropriate  discipline  and 
conduct  is  sine-quo-non.  Apprehension  of 
respondents is not without basis and stands on 
firm ground that if reinstated, it would be 
bad example for the colleagues which would be 
detrimental  to  cause  of  maintenance  of 
5

## Page 153

discipline in disciplined force like Army.
14] Further we are of the opinion that  
applicant had already been given a long rope 
by the Tribunal by way of an opportunity to 
lead evidence in Second Summary Court Martial 
but instead he exhibited disdain in availing 
the  opportunity.  This,  coupled  with  his 
earlier similar instance of OSL leaves no 
ground to allow his application. Application, 
therefore, stands dismissed.”
15. We concur with the view taken by the Tribunal. 
16. Having held so we may also mention that we are  
conscious of the decisions of this Court in Union of 
India And Others versus Vishav Priya Singh  [(2016) 8 
Supreme Court Cases 641] and Randhir Singh Vs. Union  
of India  [(2020) 14 Supreme Court Cases 513 ]. In  
Vishav Priya Singh,  this Court  had endorsed and  
affirmed the view taken by the High Court of Delhi  
that  convening  of  Summary  Court  Martial  is  an  
exception and that it is imperative that a case must  
be made out for immediacy of action. Such power must  
be exercised rarely and only when it is absolutely  
imperative  that  immediate  action  is  called  for.  
Reasons must be recorded for convening a Summary  
Court Martial. 
6

## Page 154

16.1. In Randhir Singh, this Court was concerned  
with the proceedings of a Summary Court Martial which  
dismissed the appellant after holding him guilty of  
the charge of entering into the residence of a  
colleague and placing his hands on the shoulder of  
his spouse while she was bathing her son. In the  
proceedings of  Randhir Singh , it was noted that a  
review petition was filed by Union of India for  
clarification of the decision in Vishav Priya Singh . 
In the review judgment dated 16.02.2017,  Union of  
India Vs. Vishav Priya Singh [(2020) 14 Supreme Court 
Cases 518], it has been held that the requirement of  
recording reasons for convening Summary Court Marital  
shall apply with effect from the date of the judgment  
in  Vishav  Priya  Singh  i.e.  from  05.07.2016.  
Therefore, this Court noted that the requirement of  
recording  reasons  for  convening  a  Summary  Court  
Martial would apply from 05.07.2016. However, in the 
facts and circumstances of that case, this Court found 
that  convening  of  the  Summary  Court  Martial  was 
contrary to law. Having regard to the duration of time 
which  had  elapsed  following  dismissal  of  the  
7

## Page 155

appellant from service, this Court moulded the relief  
and converted the penalty of dismissal from service  
to one of discharge and clarified that such discharge  
would take effect from the date on which appellant  
complete 15 years of service so as to render him  
eligible for grant of pension. 
17. Admittedly, the facts of the present case are  
entirely  different.  In  the  earlier  round  of  
litigation, the Tribunal had confirmed and maintained  
the order of conviction passed by the Summary Court  
Martial. This finding of the Tribunal has attained  
finality as the appellant did not assail the same. We, 
therefore, see no reason to entertain this appeal.
18. Accordingly, the Civil Appeal is dismissed.
19. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand  
disposed of.

1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This appeal impugns judgment and order of the Division
Bench of the High Court dated 13.08.2024 passed in Letters
Patent Appeal No. 617/2019 whereby the High Court had set
aside the order of the learned Single Judge dismissing writ
petition (i.e., CWJC No. 12185/2014) of the respondent
preferred against the order of dismissal from service, and
thereby directed the appellants to reinstate the respondent
in service with monetary benefits and to regularize his
absence by treating it as period spent on leave to his
credit; and thereafter, impose any minor penalty.
4. The order of the High Court has been challenged before
us primarily on the ground that there exists no dispute
that the respondent had been remained absent from duty for
1

## Page 158

a period of 196 days without leave.  It is submitted that
the respondent was part of a disciplined force and he had
to be declared a deserter and thereafter apprehended.  In
such circumstances, merely because respondent’s mother had
suffered an ailment, cannot be a ground to condone his
unauthorized absence and take a lenient view thereupon.
5. Per  contra , on behalf of respondent, it has been
submitted that the inquiry report recites the defense of
the respondent that the respondent had applied for leave on
14.05.2012 on account of his mother’s ailment; it is also
noticed in the enquiry report that the respondent had to
remain absent to attend to his ailing mother who was
diagnosed with cancer; and further, the enquiry report
recites that the respondent had been sending information
along with leave application to the concerned officer from
time to time. The stand of the respondent was disbelieved
only because the leave request letters were not produced
though the receipts regarding posting of those letter
requests were produced during the inquiry. Further, the
inquiry officer disbelieved the defense on the ground that
original medical documents were not produced though xerox
copies were produced. In such circumstances, it was argued
that findings in the inquiry report are perverse and
dismissal  from  service  is  extremely  harsh  punishment,
therefore, the High Court is justified in setting aside the
same.

inquiry the defense of the respondent was noted.  It
appears, before the inquiry officer, the respondent had
stated that due to his mother’s serious illness, he had to
leave the camp after submitting leave application and
thereafter, during the period of his absence, he had been
requesting for leave and sending information by letters.
This statement of the respondent was not accepted by the
inquiry officer on the ground that original copies of the
documents  were  not  produced.   Inquiry  officer  though
noticed the stand of the respondent that he had been
sending requests from time to time and giving information
regarding his absence on account of ailment of his mother,
disbelieved it on the ground that the request letters were
not produced. Importantly copies of the postal receipt were
produced.
10. From the recital in the inquiry report, we could
gather that the respondent had clearly set up a case of his
mother’s ailment and that his presence was required to be
with his mother to take care of her.  Further, it appears
that respondent had dispatched letters about the aforesaid
position.  Even assuming that original copies of those
medical  documents/papers  were  not  produced,  the
authenticity of those documents could not have been doubted
in absence of any controverting evidence.  Otherwise also,
those documents could have been verified by sending request
letter  to  the  institution  which  issued  those  medical
4

## Page 161

papers. Now, pursuant to our order, those documents have
been found genuine. As far as non-production of leave
request letters is concerned, suffice to say that a person
retains copy of letter when he is advised to do so or is a
person who is aware that later a dispute may arise. Here,
the respondent had produced postal receipts indicating that
dispatch of envelope(s) to the addressee was made.  Whether
those envelopes were empty, is not borne out from the
evidence.  In  such  circumstances,  the  High  Court  was
justified in holding that there was no basis to discard the
defense taken by the respondent.
11. However, we cannot ignore the fact that the respondent
was  part  of  a  disciplined  force.  Being  part  of  a
disciplined force, he ought to have acted with more care
and caution and should not have deserted the Unit without
formal grant of leave and continue to stay with his family
without formal leave. In such circumstances, the issue that
arises  for  our  consideration  is  whether  the  capital
punishment of dismissal from service was justified in the
peculiar facts of the case or not.
12. In our view, having regard to the peculiar facts of
the case, where the mother of the respondent was suffering
from cancer and she was under treatment and the respondent
had been providing information in that regard to the
officers  concerned,  the  punishment  of  dismissal  from
service is shockingly disproportionate to the gravity of
5

## Page 162

the misconduct, particularly when it is not a case of
deserting a border post and, most importantly, he had
applied  for  leave.  Therefore,  in  our  view,  a  more
compassionate view could have been taken by the department.
In such view of the matter, we do not find a good reason to
interfere with the order passed by the High Court to the
extent it sets aside the order of dismissal from service.
13. At this stage, the learned counsel representing the
Union has submitted that since admittedly the respondent
had violated the discipline of service and had remained
absent for a considerable length of time, rewarding him
with full monetary benefits would not be appropriate in the
facts of the case.  He, therefore, submits that this Court
may be pleased to modify the order passed by the High Court
and pass such appropriate order as it may deem fit.
14. Having regard to the facts of the case, we are of the
view  that  ends  of  justice  would  be  served,  if  the
respondent is deprived of his back wages during the period
he remained absent till the date of the order of the
Division Bench of the High Court. Besides, to close the
matter, in our view, it would be appropriate that he is
awarded a censure entry for the charge. The rest of the
order of the High Court is maintained. In effect, the
respondent shall be reinstated in service in terms of the
order of the Division Bench of the High Court i.e. dated
13.08.2024 and shall be provided benefits of continuity in
6

## Page 163

service but shall not be entitled to back wages as directed
above.
15. The  appeal  stands  partly  allowed  to  the  extent
indicated above.
16. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

O R D E R
1. These civil appeals by special leave, granted on 03 rd February,
2017,  challenge  the  common  judgment  and  order  dated  01st
September, 2016 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court of
Delhi at New Delhi 1 dismissing two intra-court appeals 2 of the
1  High Court
2  L.P.A. No.405/2016 and L.P.A. No.409/2016
1

## Page 199

appellants.
2. We need to note a few facts.
3. The controversy centers around release of benefits of Assured
Career Progression Scheme3 to the respondents.
4. A Single Judge of the High Court  vide judgment and order
dated  11th February,  2015  allowed  the  writ  petitions 4 of  the
respondents holding that withdrawal of benefits under the ACPS
earlier extended was wrongful. 
5. Challenging the judgment and order dated 11 th February,
2015, the appellants preferred an intra-court appeal 5 before the High
Court. The order passed on the said appeal dated 28 th July, 2015
reads as follows:
“1. After some arguments learned counsel for the appellant
states that the appeal may be permitted to be withdrawn with
an observation that if the appellant seeks review of the
impugned order dated February 11, 2015 the learned Single
Judge may be requested to decide the same as per law and be
considerate in condoning the delay in seeking the review.
2. Accordingly we dismiss the appeal as not pressed observing
that if the appellant seeks review of the order dated February
11, 2015 the learned Single Judge shall bestow a consideration
thereto as per the review jurisdiction of the Court and as
regards the delay in seeking review the learned Single Judge
would decide the sufficiency of the cause for delay to be
condoned as pleaded.”
3  ACPS
4  W.P. (C) No. 2118 of 2012 and W.P. (C) No. 2117 of 2012
5  LPA 484/2015
2

## Page 200

6. Availing the liberty granted by the High Court in the aforesaid
order dated 28 th July, 2015, the appellants applied for review. The
review petition, however, came to be dismissed by an order dated
14th March, 2016 of the Single Judge.
7. The order dated 14th March, 2016 rejecting the review as well
as the parent order dated 11 th February, 2015 allowing the writ
petition were once again carried in appeal before the High Court
which, as noticed above, has rejected the intra-court appeals.
8. We need not express any opinion on the merits of the decision
given by the Division Bench, for, in our opinion, the intra-court
appeals in the first place were not maintainable; and, the Division
Bench without even examining the challenge on merits could have
dismissed the same by referring to the principles flowing from the
Code of Civil Procedure, 19086.
9. From the extract of the order dated 28 th July, 2015, it is clear
that while electing to have the intra-court appeal dismissed as not
pressed and, on the contrary, seeking liberty to apply before the
Single Judge for review, the appellants did neither seek nor were
granted leave by the Division Bench to challenge the order dated 11 th
February, 2015 of the Single Judge, over again, should the review fail.
10. Once leave was not obtained to challenge the order dated 11 th
February, 2015 of the Single Judge over again, principles flowing from
Order XXIII Rule 1 of the CPC were attracted. The second intra-court
6  CPC
3

## Page 201

appeal against the order dated 11 th February, 2015 was, thus
incompetent ab initio.
11. We may refer to the decisions of this Court in M/s. Upadhyay
& Company Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh 7 and Satheesh V.K. v.
Federal Bank Ltd. 8 where this Court, in the context of previous
withdrawal of special leave petitions without permission to move for
special leave subsequently, declined interference. The law laid down
therein squarely applies here. The same order cannot be challenged
over again without leave of the Court before which the claim was
abandoned/not pressed. 
12. Insofar as the challenge to the order passed by the Single
Judge dismissing the review petition is concerned, no appeal lay
under Order XLVII Rule 7, CPC; a fortiori, no appeal before this Court
in the absence of any valid appeal against the order, of which review
was sought, would independently be maintainable.
13. Since either of the two appeals before the Division Bench of
the High Court was not maintainable, we see no reason to entertain
the present appeals for examining the merits of the orders under
challenge.
14. In such view of the matter, the civil appeals stand dismissed.
15. We are also not inclined to interfere with the order under
challenge in SLP (C) No. 11556/2018 which, too, stands dismissed.

1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. The  present  appeal is directed  against the order dated 20.11.2025
passed by the High  Court  of judicature for Rajasthan  at Jaipur Bench,
whereunder  the  prayer  of  the  appellant  for  quashing  of  the  criminal
proceedings pending against him has been dismissed.
4.  Facts  in  brief  which  has  led  to  the  filing  of  this  appeal  can  be
crystallized as under:
The  case  of  the  prosecution  is  to  the  effect  that  appellant  as
Director of M/s. Himanshu Garments Private Limited and he had entered
into a criminal conspiracy with UCO Bank officials and approved valuers
1                                                                                        SLP(CRL.) NO.11999 OF 2026

## Page 227

and  submitted  over-valued  collateral  properties  (including  heritage
properties and properties in Delhi) and had forged foreign purchase orders
for  securing  packing  credit  limits  and  post  shipment  credit  limits  far
exceeding the permissible limits. It is also alleged by the prosecution that
appellant created  a sister concern  by  name  M/s. Meenakshi Garments
Private Limited using his brother as a front to extract additional loans and
these actions of the appellant caused a wrongful loss to over 4.27 crores
to UCO Bank. The Respondent-CBI filed a chargesheet against appellant
and seven other accused. 
On account of the appellant’s prolonged absence, appellant’s bail
bond was canceled by order dated 23.08.2014 by the learned Special
Judge and appellant was declared a proclaimed offender/absconder vide
order dated 05.01.2015. After full fledged trial against the other accused
and after splitting up the chargesheet against the appellant herein, the
jurisdictional court examined the claim of the prosecution and arrived at a
conclusion that prosecution had failed to prove conspiracy, forgery and
criminal  misconduct  beyond  reasonable  doubt  by  judgment  dated
31.08.2018 and thereby acquitted them. 
5. Being aggrieved by the same the respondent-CBI is said to have filed
an  appeal  before  the  High  Court  in  S  B  Criminal  Leave  to  Appeal
No235/2019 and it is said to be pending.
6. In the light of the trial court acquitting the other accused, the appellant
suddenly  woke  up  from  his  slumber  and  invoked  the  extra-ordinary
jurisdiction of the High Court under Section 482 CrPC for quashing of the
proceedings against him on the ground of continuation of trial against him
would be an abuse of process of law and the prosecution evidence against
2                                                                                        SLP(CRL.) NO.11999 OF 2026

## Page 228

the appellant, as pitted against other accused persons, is inseparable. It
was  also  contended  that  in  view  of  all  other  accused  having  been
acquitted, continuation of prosecution against the appellant herein was
not warranted. It was further contended that absence of the appellant
before was not intentional but due to medical issues resulting from an
accident that occurred in United States of America (USA) and purported
communication gap with his trial court advocate.
7. Evidentiary value pitted against the accused who has been acquitted
vis-a-vis the evidence against appellant relied upon would be an issue
which will have to be examined only after full fledged trial. At this stage,
this Court would not be in a position to evaluate the same and neither the
High Court under exercise of jurisdiction under Section 482 CrPC could
undertake such an exercise. As to how the evidence that has been relied
upon by the prosecution against those of the accused who have been
acquitted  would  be  inseparable,  is  an  issue  which  will  have  to  be
examined  only  after  evidence  that  is  being  relied  upon  against  the
appellant, is tendered by the prosecution before the jurisdictional trial
court. Here is a person, namely, appellant, who has been absconding for
17 long years and only after other accused persons were acquitted, seems
to have gained knowledge of the same and invoked the extra-ordinary
jurisdiction  of  the  High  Court  for  quashing  the  proceedings  pending
against him. The High Court has rightly refused to quash the proceedings
and we do not find any infirmity in the findings recorded by the High Court
in that regard.
8. Be that as it may . On account of there being a warrant of arrest issued
against  the  appellant,  apprehending  his  arrest,  the  appellant  had  not
appeared before the jurisdictional trial court, or in other words, he did not
3                                                                                        SLP(CRL.) NO.11999 OF 2026

## Page 229

intent  to  arrive  in  this  country  to  face  the  trial  initiated  against  him.
Hence, to secure his presence and to ensure that the trial progresses
expeditiously and to allay the apprehension of the appellant that he would
not be arrested, this Court by order dated 03.07.2026 had stayed the
arrest warrant issued against the appellant. Yet the jurisdictional Court
seems to have proceeded on a technical ground to take the appellant into
custody  and  the  learned  ASG  appearing  for the  respondent-CBI would
submit  that  the  warrant  has  not  been  executed  and  it  is  only  the
jurisdictional  Court  which  has  proceeded  to  take  the  appellant  into
custody for proceeding with the trial. We do not propose to enter into any
issue on this aspect. The fact remains that despite the arrest warrant
stayed by this Court, or in other words, the order was to the effect that no
coercive steps shall be taken against the appellant, yet he was taken into
custody, which cannot be accepted.
9. Hence, appellant is ordered to be released on bail on such terms and
conditions as the jurisdictional court may deem fit to impose including the
condition of surrendering the passport during the trial and also on the
condition  that  he  shall  not  leave  the  jurisdiction  of  the  Court  without
express permission from the said Court and shall appear before the trial
court  on  all  dates  of  hearing  without  fail,  except  when  specifically
exempted.
10. With these observations, the prayer for quashing of the proceedings is
rejected and is granted interim bail during the pendency of the trial as
observed hereinabove. Accordingly, the appeal stands allowed in part.

O R D E R
1. Appellant  was  compulsorily  retired  from  service  following
disciplinary proceedings. 
2. Challenge before the Single Judge of the High Court of Judicature
at Allahabad1 failed; the writ petition 2 was dismissed by a judgment and
order dated 04th March, 2016. Appellant having preferred an appeal3, the
same also stood dismissed by a judgment and order dated 11 th May,
2016 of the Division Bench.
3. This appeal, by special leave granted on 23 rd September, 2016, is
directed against the Division Bench’s judgment and order.
4. Learned senior counsel for the appellant has raised three points:
(i) Mr. Amit Kumar,  Additional Chief Executive  Officer at Cantonment
1 High Court
2 Civil Misc. Writ Petition No.4181 of 2014
3 Special Appeal No.299 of 2016
1

## Page 234

Board,  Kanpur  had  no  jurisdiction  to  issue  the  order  of  compulsory
retirement;  (ii)  principles  of  natural  justice  were  breached  because
despite the Inquiry Officer having allowed the prayer of the appellant for
summoning Sri N. V . Satyanarayan, Navendra Nath and Neeraj Jain as
defence witnesses, he recalled such order without any reason; and (iii)
the  appellant  was  figuring  as  an  accused  in  a  criminal  case  which
ultimately resulted in filing of a closure report and since the incident
giving  rise  to  the  First  Information  Report  and  the  departmental
chargesheet, the documentary evidence and the oral evidence were the
same, the High Court ought to have set the disciplinary proceedings at
naught.   
5. We  have  not  considered  it  necessary  to  call  upon  the
respondents to answer.
6. Insofar  as  the  first  point  is  concerned,  we  find  that  Mr.  Amit
Kumar  had  been  transferred  as  Additional  Chief  Executive  Officer  at
Cantonment  Board,  Kanpur  from  the  post  of  Defence  Estate  Officer,
Bhopal. It was due to an administrative exigency that such a transfer
had been effected. Mr. Amit Kumar joined at Kanpur without raising any
objection.
7. It  is  not  disputed  before  us  that  the  post  of  Defence  Estate
Officer is a post higher than the post of Chief Executive Officer of the
Cantonment Board, being the appellant’s appointing authority . 
8. We, therefore, hold that Mr. Amit Kumar did have the jurisdiction
to pass the order of compulsory retirement. 
2

## Page 235

9. Regarding  complaint of breach of natural justice, which  is the
second  point  argued  before  us,  we  find  that  the  appellant  had  not
indicated why presence of the said three persons was relevant for the
purpose of the inquiry . Besides, it was open to the appellant to produce
the said three persons in the enquiry since they were cited as defence
witnesses  by  him.  Attempt  of  the  appellant  to  seek  their  presence
without indicating relevance, and that too almost on the verge of close
of enquiry, was clearly an afterthought to delay the enquiry . 
10. Having regard to the law laid down by the High Court at Calcutta
in paragraph 27 of its decision in A.R.S. Choudhury v. The Union of
India  and  Ors.4, which we do hereby endorse, the point argued on
behalf  of  the  appellant  (without  demonstrating  relevance  of  such
witnesses) lacks substance and, accordingly, is rejected.
11. T urning  to  the  third  point,  we  find  that  the  appellant  was
proceeded against for lack of devotion to perform his duty . That could
never have formed a charge in the criminal case. The circumstance that
the  genesis  of  an  FIR  and  a  departmental  chargesheet  is  the  same
cannot  be  accepted  as  a  ground  to  hold  that  an  enquiry  under  the
service rules is barred. That apart, law is well settled that even acquittal
in  a criminal case would  not  bar a disciplinary  proceeding  since the
standard  of proof in a criminal proceeding  varies  from  a disciplinary
proceeding. 
12. Having regard to the findings recorded by the High Court in the
4 AIR 1956 Cal 662
3

## Page 236

penultimate paragraph of the impugned judgment, we see no warrant
for any interference in exercise of our jurisdiction under Article 136 of
the Constitution of India. 
13. The  civil  appeal  is  devoid  of  merits  and  is,  accordingly,
dismissed.
14. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

Caste  category  in  the  Market  Plan  2013-14.  Applications  were

qualified, the others being held to be not qualified. However, the
third respondent, on scrutiny, was not able to satisfy one of the
conditions,  i.e.:  maintenance  of  Rs.5,00,000/-  as  balance  in  the
savings  bank  account.  A  letter  was  issued  by  the  respondent
Corporation to the third respondent to clarify, which was replied with
an admission that the bank account contained only Rs.28,500/-. The
Corporation carried out a re-scrutiny of the applications of the other
applicants and selected the appellant herein. The litigation arose on

## Page 240

2
such allotment being granted to the appellant. 
3. Admittedly, the appellant has been carrying on the dealership
having  established  it  in  the  year  2016.  The  writ  petition  was
dismissed and later the writ appeal was allowed by the impugned
judgment  in  the  year  2018.  The  appellant  continued  based  on
interim orders issued by this Court and today the matter is taken up
for hearing.
4. The  writ  petition  was  rejected  on  the  ground  that  the  writ
petitioner, third respondent herein had absolutely no  locus  standi.

appeal was filed by the third respondent, which was allowed by the
Division Bench.
5. Even before the Division Bench, the issue of locus standi  was
raised but the Division Bench brushed it aside and looked at the
procedure followed by the respondent Nos.1 and 2, especially since
the respondent is carrying out a public duty and the dealership grant
will be largesse to the grantee, which has to be equitably and fairly
allotted. It was found that there was no procedure to carry out a re-
scrutiny of the already disqualified applicants.

## Page 241

3
6. The Corporation filed a review pointing out the communication
of the Government of India, Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas
dated 25.02.2016. According to them this conferred authority on the
corporation  to  carry  out  a  re-scrutiny  without  a  corrigendum  or
addendum  to  the  advertisement  already  published.  On  going
through  Annexure  P13,  the  communication  relied  on  by  the
Corporation, we are not inclined to find that such an exercise was
permitted,  insofar  as  disqualified  applicants  are  concerned.
However, the re-scrutiny had been carried out, and the applicant
was selected and he was allotted the dealership, which commenced
in 2016 and carried on till today without any complaint.
7. The direction in the impugned judgment was to carry out a
fresh  advertisement.  Having  established  the  dealership,  a  fresh
advertisement  now  carried  out  would  only  result  in  further
expenditure by the Corporation, which again would be a drain on
public money.  Though  we  are  of the  opinion  that the  procedure
carried  out  was  not  permitted  by  the  document  produced  as
Annexure P13, there can be no dispute as to the applicant having
qualified every aspect of eligibility at least in the re-scrutiny, since
he was permitted to establish the dealership and he is running the
same till date.

## Page 242

4
8. We  were also told that the dealership  was run without any
problem in all these years. What assumes significance is the locus
standi of the third respondent, having not been considered by the
Appellate  Court.  The  learned  Single  Judge  had  rejected  the  writ
petition on the ground of locus standi, and we are also of the opinion
that  the  third  respondent  had  no  locus  standi  to  challenge  the
allotment, since he was a disqualified applicant and he could not
raise the issue as a public interest also.
9. Considering the totality of the circumstances, we are inclined to
set aside the order of the Division Bench only considering the fact
that third respondent had no locus standi  and the more compelling
reason  of the appellant having continued  with the dealership  all
these years.
10. The appeals stand allowed only on the ground of continuation
of the dealership in the intervening period.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
