IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.3832 OF 2026
(Arising out of S.L.P.(Criminal) No.1696 of 2026)
GAURAV AIREN & ORS.  ... APPELLANT(S) 
                  VS.
THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH ... RESPONDENT(S)
     
                                                                   
          O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard  Mr.  Raghvendra  Dixit,  learned  counsel
appearing  for  the  appellants  and  Mr.  Yashraj  Singh
Bundela, learned counsel appearing for the respondent-
State.
3. The  present  appeal calls  in  question  the
correctness of the judgment and order dated 16th December,
2025 passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh, Bench at
Gwalior in Miscellaneous Criminal Case No.49589 of 2024.
By the said order, the High Court dismissed the petition
filed  under  Section  482  of  the  Code  of  Criminal
Procedure, 1973 by the appellants challenging the order
dated 21 st August, 2023 passed by the Chief Judicial
Magistrate, Morena, Madhya Pradesh by which cognizance
was taken against the appellants.
1

## Page 252

4. The appellants are the Directors of a company, by
name, M/s. IVES Drugs (India) Private Limited situated at
Ghatabillod, District Dhar, Madhya Pradesh.  The company
manufactures a drug by name Sodium Lactate Injection.  On
a  complaint  by  the  Civil  Surgeon-cum-Chief  Hospital
Superintendent, District Hospital, Morena, to the Drug
Inspector,  Morena,  sample  of  the  drug  bearing B atch
No.10311 was sent to the Central Drug Testing Laboratory,
Calcutta.  It appears that the Central Drug Testing
Laboratory, Calcutta analyzed the drug and found that the
drug  was not  of standard  quality. According  to the
appellants, the test report was sent after a period of
107 days which was against the mandatory provision under
Rule 45 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 which
mandates a 60 days timeline.  The appellants contended
that this vitiated the prosecution.
5. A complaint was filed by the Drug Inspector against
the appellants without arraying the company as a party
for the offences punishable under Sections 18(a)(1) and
27(d) of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 (for short,
“the 1940 Act”).  The cognizance was taken on 21 st August,
2023  resulting  in  the  quash  petition  being  filed.
Manifold contentions were raised by the appellants.
2

## Page 253

6. Primarily, it was contented that the company has
not been made a party and in the absence of the company,
a  complaint  was  not  maintainable.  It  was  further
contended that there was no averment in the complaint to
fulfill the ingredients of Section 34 and to attract the
ingredients of Section 18 and 27 of the 1940 Act.  
7. As  stated  earlier,  it  was  also  alleged  that
timelines were violated in sending the result of the test
report.
8. From perusal of the impugned order, we notice  that
after setting out the contentions and the authorities
cited in detail, there is no discussion or analysis on
two of the three contentions set out herein above.  The
High Court got over the contention of the non-impleadment
of the company by directing the Trial Court to in-turn
communicate with  the concerned Drug Inspector and join
the company as a party respondent.  The High Court ought
to have decided whether the non-joining of the company
was fatal for the complainant or not. Instead at the post
cognizance stage, it directed the impleadment of the
company.  Secondly, the aspect of the timelines being
violated in furnishing the test report has not been
discussed.
3

## Page 254

9. Insofar as the aspect dealing with the necessary
averments  in  the  complaint,  though  the  High  Court
referred to all the precedents that were cited by the
appellants, there is no effort made in the judgment to
apply the judgment to the facts or to distinguish the
same. We are of the opinion that the matter requires to
be  remitted  back  to  the  High  Court  for  a  fresh
consideration.
10. We have not expressed any opinion on the merits of
the case.  We have also not expressed any opinion on the
correctness of the procedure adopted by the High Court in
directing joining of the company at the post cognizance
stage.  The High Court may take a fresh call on the same.
Since the appellants have placed their case on more than
one count, we are left with no other option but to remand
the matter to the High Court for a fresh consideration of
Section 482 petition.
11. For the reasons stated above, we set aside the
impugned order dated 16 th December, 2025 passed by the
High Court in Miscellaneous Criminal Case No.49589 of
2024.   The  consequence  will  be  that  Miscellaneous
Criminal Case No.49589 of 2024 will stand restored to the
file of the High Court of Madhya Pradesh, Bench at
Gwalior for a fresh consideration in accordance with law.
4

## Page 255

12. The appeal is disposed of in the above terms.
13. On 2 nd February, 2026, this Court had stayed the
proceedings in Case No.1717 of 2023 pending before the
Chief Judicial Magistrate, Morena, Madhya Pradesh.  We
continue the said order for a period of four weeks from
today.  The appellants are at liberty to move the High
Court for further interim orders.
14. Considering the nature of the matter, we request
the High Court to make an endeavour to dispose of the
matter as expeditiously as possible.
..........................J.
       (K.V.VISWANATHAN)
                          
 ..........................J.
       (ARUN PALLI) 
NEW DELHI;
August 11, 2026

1. Heard. 
2. Leave granted.
3. The prosecution has alleged that on 08.11.2023 at
around 08:25 p.m., the appellant under the influence of
alcohol started urinating in front of the informant’s house
to which Smt. Shanti Devi (grandmother of the informant)
objected and at that point of time, the appellant called his
associates Balveer Singh, Ramkaran @ Bablu and others
and incited them to attack her. It is further alleged that
1

## Page 258

unlawful group so assembled had assaulted Smt. Shanti
Devi,  her  son  –  Udayveer  Singh  and  daughter-in-law  –
Laxmi Devi with lathis, dandas and iron rod and due to the
injuries sustained, Smt. Shanti Devi expired and as such FIR
No.452/2023 came to be registered against the appellant
and others for the offences punishable under Sections 302,
323 and 504 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
4. After  completion  of  the  investigation,  chargesheet
has been filed citing thirty-three witnesses and trial has
commenced and two witnesses have been examined. The
appellant has been in custody since 23.11.2023 till date.
5. Having heard the learned counsels appearing for the
parties, we notice that PW-1 – the informant has deposed
that Balveer Singh, son of Pratap Singh struck a lathi blow
on the head of his grandmother Smt. Shanti Devi (who is
said to have succumbed to the injuries sustained). Yet,
surprisingly, the prosecution has not filed any chargesheet
against him and only the appellant has been arraigned as
an accused on the ground that he   instigated others to
attack.
2

## Page 259

6. Though  the  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
appellant  would  vehemently  contend  that  there  is  a
political rivalry and the evidence of PW-1 and PW-2 would
also  indicate  that  the  mother  of  the  informant  had
contested for the election of Pradhan of the village of which
village the appellant’s mother is now the present Pradhan.
These are issues, if examined at this stage, which are likely
to prejudice the rights of the prosecution also and as such
we desist from delving upon it.
7. Suffice to state that apprehension of the prosecution
that the appellant is likely to indulge in either threatening
or  influencing  the  witnesses  can  be  safely  allayed  by
putting  him  on  strictest  terms,  namely,  prohibiting  the
appellant from entering the village – Madhaa machi Jheel,
P.S. Bidhuna, District – Auraiya, Uttar Pradesh till conlusion
of trial and also imposing the condition of appellant should
not contact or induce or influence or threaten any of the
witnesses during the trial. We also make it clear that the
jurisdictional court would be at liberty to impose such other
and further condition as it deems fit in addition to what has
3

## Page 260

been indicated hereinabove. With these observations, the
appeal stands allowed, the impugned order is set aside and
the appellant is ordered to be released on bail subject to
the observations made and condition imposed hereinabove
and subject to such other and further conditions as the trial
court may deem fit to impose. 
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
.................J.
  (ARAVIND KUMAR)
.................J.
(VIPUL M. PANCHOLI)
NEW DELHI;
AUGUST 12, 2026.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS.         /2026
 [@ SLP [CRL.] NO.6257-6258/2026]
SUNIL KUMAR                          Appellant(s)
VERSUS
CENTRAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION     Respondent(s)
O R D E R
Leave granted.
Aggrieved over the condition imposed by the
High Court while granting anticipatory bail in
connection  with  FIR  No.RC-06(A)/2019-R  dated
14.11.2019,  registered  at  Police  Station  –

## Page 288

2
CBI/ACB,  District  Ranchi  for  the  offences
punishable under Section 120-B read with Sections
409, 420, 467, 468 and 471 of the Indian Penal
Code, 1860 and Section 13(2) read with Section
13(1)(c) and (d) of the Prevention of Corruption
Act,  1988,  the  appellant  has  approached  this
Court. The High Court has granted anticipatory
bail to the appellant on the condition that he
deposit  Rs.65,00,000/-  with  the  Deputy
Commissioner. 
We have heard the learned counsel appearing
for the parties.
Learned counsel appearing for the appellant
submitted that it has been repeatedly held by this
Court that onerous conditions which are impossible
to be complied with cannot be imposed upon the
accused by the Courts while granting bail.
Learned ASG appearing for the State submitted
that having accepted the condition imposed, it is
not open to the appellant to turn back on it.
We are inclined to hold that the condition

## Page 289

3
imposed  by  the  High  Court  herein  is  totally
unwarranted. No effort has been made to find out
as to whether the appellant was even in a position
to comply with the said condition. This is not the
first  case  that  we  are  seeing  where  such
conditions have been imposed. We are constrained
to note that conditions of this nature are being
imposed by the courts as a matter of course while
granting  bail  which  has  to  be  avoided.  The
anticipatory  bail  applications  and  bail
applications will have to be decided on their own
merits and the laying down of such conditions is
only an additional factor. Such conditions can be
imposed only when the situation so warrants and
the accused person is capable of compliance.
Considering  the  facts  governing,  we  are
inclined  to  set  aside  the  impugned  condition
imposed  by  the  High  Court  while  granting
anticipatory  bail  to  the  appellant  vide  the
impugned order.

## Page 290

4
Accordingly, the impugned order(s) stand set
aside only qua the impugned condition.
The appeals stand allowed, accordingly.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.
...............….J.
[M.M. SUNDRESH]
...................J.

O R D E R
1. This contempt proceeding has been initiated for alleged willful disobedience
of the order of this Court dated 20.01.2026 passed in SLP(C) No.4310/2025 by
contending that pursuant to the oral observations made by this Court, the
affidavit dated 02.02.2026 was filed and as admitted thereunder same is not
being complied and hence there is willful disobedience. 
2. Howsoever attractive the arguments may be, this Court cannot invoke the
contempt jurisdiction in the absence of there being any positive direction and
there being willful disobedience of such order or direction.
3. In the instant case, in the order dated 20.01.2026, there is no such direction
issued and if at all any affidavit is filed by the respondent(s) to do any particular
act, it will be open to the complainant to pursue his grievance before
appropriate forum for appropriate relief, if not already initiated.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Heard learned counsel for the parties. 
2. On 21.07.2026, by noticing the controversy that required our
1

## Page 324

consideration,  we  had  passed  a  detailed  order,  which  is
reproduced herein below:
“1. The submission on behalf of the learned counsel
for the petitioner is that neither the Service Rules,
1979 nor the Recruitment Advertisement provided that
work experience in a State Forensic Laboratory or
Central Forensic Laboratory or in a Public Sector Unit
would have to be in the field/division concerned. In
such circumstances, when it is the admitted case of
the respondents that the petitioner had obtained marks
above  the  cut  off  fixed  for  the  post  of  Senior
Scientific  Officer  (Toxicology)  and  possess  the
minimum academic qualification specified in the Rules
as well as in the Recruitment Notice, he could not
have been denied appointment on the ground that his
work experience in the Forensic Science laboratory was
not in the concerned division. In support of his
submission, the learned counsel for the petitioner has
placed before us the relevant Rules as well as the
Schedule to the Rules and the Recruitment Notice.
2.  The  Recruitment  Notice  for  the  purpose  of
eligibility to the post of Senior Scientific Officer
(Toxicology) mentions essential qualification “M.Sc
IInd  division  in  Chemistry  from  a  University
established by Law in India; and (b) Two year’s
experience of working in a Forensic Science Laboratory
of a State or Central Government or similar experience
in Public Undertaking or Corporation.
3. Prima facie, it appears, there is no specific
requirement of experience in a particular division of
the Forensic Science Laboratory of a State or Central
Government.
4. The learned counsel representing the respondent
submits that both qualifications are provided under
one heading in the Schedule to the Rules. The first
part relates to educational qualification and the
second  part  relates  to  experience  in  a  Forensic
Science Laboratory. In such circumstances, it would be
deemed that the experience must relate to the field in
respect  of  which  educational  qualification  is
required. Accordingly, it has been submitted on behalf
of the respondents that the Recruiting Department had
issued a clarificatory letter to the Public Service
Commission stating therein that experience in the
concerned division would alone be considered and not
general experience in the Forensic Science Laboratory.
5.  At  this  stage,  the  learned  counsel  for  the
petitioner placed before us the certificate issued by
Central Forensic Science Laboratory, Central Bureau of
Investigation, New Delhi regarding the work experience
of the petitioner. Relying on that certificate, the
learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the
work experience certificate does not reflect work in
any particular division though it reflects experience
of working on a specified post. In such circumstances,
it has been submitted that there was no requirement of
2

## Page 325

work  in  any  particular  division  of  the  Forensic
Science Laboratory; the work experience would have to
relate only to the number of years in a particular
Forensic  Science  Laboratory,  which  the  petitioner
fulfils.
6. Having regard to the above submissions, before we
finally decide the matter, we need clarification on
two aspects:
(i) Whether the posts advertised, in respect of which
the petitioner had applied and found above the cutoff
for selection, are still vacant or have been filled
up?;
(ii) Whether Forensic Science Laboratory of the State
and the Central Government have separate divisions. If
so,  whether  Forensic  Science  Laboratories  issue
certificate  of  work  experience  in  a  particular
division or on a post?
  
7.  List  these  matters  for  further  hearing  on
12.08.2026.” 
3. Pursuant to the above order, the learned counsel for the
petitioner has filed an affidavit annexing therewith certain
documents including an RTI query to indicate that in the past
there have been no appointments on  division specific basis,
particularly for the post of Laboratory Assistant. He has also
invited our attention to Annexure P-21 which is a clarificatory
letter dated 04.02.2020 issued by the Government of Rajasthan.
By  pointing  to  that  letter,  it  has  been  submitted  that
clarification regarding division specific experience came later
i.e., after the advertisement. 
4. Per  contra, on behalf of the respondents, it is submitted
that the Central Forensic Science Laboratory as well as State
Forensic Science Laboratory have specific divisions such as
Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Serology, Ballistics, Documents,
Finger Prints, Forensic Psychology, Photo, Computer Forensic
Science & Scientific Aids divisions etc.  It is submitted that
the post in question is one of Senior Scientific Officer,
3

## Page 326

Poison  Division  (i.e.,  Toxicology).  The  said  division  is
related to chemistry. Since chemistry division is separate from
the photo division, the work experience of the petitioner in
the photo division would not inure to his eligibility for the
post in question.
5. We have considered the rival submissions and have also
taken note of the clarificatory letter dated 04.02.2020. The
clarification contained therein is in the following terms: 
“The statutory provisions contemplated in the
schedule (S. No. 8 to 13, column-4) appended
to the Rajasthan Forensic Science Service
Rules, 1979, are apparent in itself, which
requires two years' experience of working in
a F.S.L. of a State or Central Government or
similar experience in a public undertaking or
corporation  (except  SSO,  Photo  Division)
only. It does not envisage specifying the
same on a division basis.”
6. A perusal of the aforesaid clarification would indicate
that  the  clarification  was  in  respect  of  an  obvious
understanding  of  the  existing  division  specific  experience
which needed no mention. As to what qualification is required,
and how a qualification specified is to be understood, must be
left to the employer unless the understanding is in teeth of
statutory  rules  or  advertisement.  Admittedly,  there  are
specific  divisions  in  the  Forensic  Science  Laboratories,
therefore if the employer seeks work experience in a particular
division for appointment on higher post in that division, the
decision of the employer cannot be held arbitrary. In such
circumstances, it cannot be said that the clarification seeks
to  amend  the  existing  rule  or  the  conditions  in  the
4

## Page 327

advertisement. Rather, it clarifies the position that exists by
emphasizing  that  experience  must  fall  in  the  concerned
division. 
7. Having regard to the above, we are of the view that the
order passed by the High Court does not call for interference.
8. The Special Leave Petitions are, accordingly, dismissed.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

1. We have heard learned counsel for the applicant(s)  
as  well  as  learned  counsel  for  National  Highways

2. This  Miscellaneous  Application  has  been  filed  
seeking the following relief(s):
“A. Modify the order dated 16.01.2025 passed  
by this Hon'ble Court in Civil Appeal No. 423  
of 2025 arising out of SLP(C) No. 27299 of  
2024, titled National Highways Authority of  
India v. Tribhavan Kumar Jain & Ors., to the  
limited  extent  that  the  requirement  of  
furnishing a bank guarantee of a nationalised  
bank for release of 50% of the compensation  
amount may be dispensed with/substituted;
B. Direct that 50% of the compensation amount  
1

## Page 329

be released to the Applicants/Respondent Nos.  
1  to  4  upon  furnishing  adequate  security  
comprising title deeds/ownership documents of  
equivalent value/security of their own land or  
security furnished by any other landowner by  
submitting title papers, to the satisfaction  
of the learned Executing Court;
C. Direct that the remaining 50% amount shall  
continue to remain invested in fixed deposit  
with a nationalised bank and renewed from time  
to time till disposal of the appeal before the  
High  Court,  as  already  directed  by  this  
Hon'ble Court vide order dated 16.01.2025.”
3. It may be mentioned that in Civil Appeal No.420 of  
2025 instituted by the NHAI, this Court passed the  
order dated 16.01.2025 which reads thus:
“Leave granted.
The impugned orders are modified to a limited  
extent. It will be open for the executing  
Court  to  disburse  50  per  cent  of  the  
compensation amount to the claimants against a  
bank guarantee of a nationalised bank to be  
furnished by the claimants to the satisfaction  
of the executing Court. The remaining amount  
shall be invested in a fixed deposit with any  
nationalised bank and the fixed deposit shall  
2

## Page 330

be renewed from time to time till the disposal  
of the appeals before the High Court.
The Appeals are partly allowed on the above  
terms.”
4. We find that in an identical matter being Special  
Leave Petition (Civil) Diary No. 2998/2026 [National  
Highways  Authority  of  India  versus  Indian  Acrylics 
Limited & Ors.], a co-ordinate Bench of this Court  
while disposing of the matter on 02.02.2026 had passed  
the following order:
3. Having heard the learned counsel for the  
NHAI, and with a view to expedite the release  
of compensation amount to the land owners, we  
deem  it  appropriate  to  dispose  of  these  
Special Leave Petitions with a clarification  
that the 'adequate security' may be security  
comprising title deeds/ownership documents of  
equivalent value, to the satisfaction of the  
executing court, but such ‘adequate security’  
shall not be in the form of a bank guarantee.
5. We  are  of  the  view  that  furnishing  of  bank  
guarantee of a Nationalized Bank to the extent of 50%  
of the compensation awarded to the claimant(s) would be  
harsh; after all, applicant(s) are the land owner(s) of  
the land(s).
3

## Page 331

6. In such circumstances and having regard to the  
peculiar facts of this case, it would be just and  
proper to substitute the requirement of bank guarantee  
by adequate security which may be by way of title  
deeds/ownership documents of equivalent value etc.
7. With the above clarification, the Interlocutory  
Application is disposed of.
8. The Miscellaneous Application is allowed.
9. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand  
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.                OF 2026

BUCHIYA DEVI & ORS. ..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
THE STATE OF BIHAR     ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellants who have been arraigned as accused in FIR No.35 of 2023
for the offence punishable under Sections 363 and 365 IPC, are before
this Court seeking anticipatory bail after their prayer has been rejected
by the Courts below.
4.  Having heard the learned counsels appearing for the parties, we
notice that omnibus allegations is made against the appellants viz.,
they have abducted the victim-Rakhi Kumari who was married to
accused no.2 (Subhash Mandal), namely, the son of Appellant Nos.1
and 3 and husband of Appellant No.2 and it is also alleged that during
1         SLP(CRL.) NO.3024 OF 2026

## Page 334

the subsistence of the marriage with the victim-Rakhi Kumari, Appellant
Nos.1 and 3 in connivance with Appellant No.2 had performed the
marriage with accused No.1 and as such the victim had lodged several
cases and while she was proceeding to depose in the said cases, she
had been abducted and her whereabouts are not known till date.
5. The role attributed to the appellants seems that Rakhi Kumari
(victim) who was married to Subhash Mandal was subjected to cruelty
by her husband and in-laws and from 20.02.2023 she went missing and
complainant suspected that her husband Subhash Mandal and his
family members including the other co-accused had abducted her with
intent to eliminate her.
6. Perusal of the impugned order would indicate that it lacks reasons. In
fact, this Court in the case of Mahipal v Rajesh Kumar alias Polia , 2020
2 SCC 118, has clearly held that judicial orders must record the reasons
and the factora that weighed with the Court  either in granting or
refusing bail, the said element is conspicuously absent in the instant
case namely in the impugned order. Only on the ground of nature of
offence, the prayer for bail has been rejected. In fact, appellants claim
to be residing separately from that of their son. The said issue is not
being examined by this Court and it is for the jurisdictional trial Court to
examine the same after full-fledged trial. In fact, this Court while issuing
notice in the present petition had granted an interim protection from
any coercive steps being taken against the appellants subject to their
cooperation with the investigation and no material is placed to
demonstrate that appellants have refused to cooperate with the
investigation.
2         SLP(CRL.) NO.3024 OF 2026

## Page 335

7.  In thee circumstances, we are of the considered view that appeal
deserves to be allowed. Hence, the appeal is allowed. Impugned order
is set aside. Appellants are ordered to be released on anticipatory bail
on such terms and conditions as the jurisdictional Investigating Officer
(IO) may deem fit to impose and also on the condition that appellant
would appear before the IO for investigation as and when called and
they shall also appear before the trial court on all dates of hearing
except when exempted for any specific reason.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

1. An additional affidavit has been filed on behalf of the
home buyers in which it is stated that despite direction of
this Court dated 19.09.2025 to handover units within 60
days, the first respondent has failed to handover physical
possession of flats to numerous buyers despite having
received the entire payment a year ago. List of those home
buyers has been annexed as Annexure ‘A’ to the affidavit.
It has also been alleged that the first respondent is
guilty of diverting funds and resources to launch a new
project of which details are provided in paragraph 3.  In
paragraph 4, it is stated that the podium of the project is
not yet complete and there is absolutely no connectivity to
Tower ‘H’.  In paragraph 5, it is stated that lifts are not
3

## Page 346

maintained and in Towers ‘G’ and ‘H’ only two lifts are
operational. Besides, even though two generator sets are
provided only one is functioning.  In paragraph 6, it is
stated that the first respondent had collected Rs.2.5
crores towards Club House Amenities but those amenities are
yet to be provided, and they remain non-functional till
date.  In paragraph 7 of the affidavit, it is stated that
since there has been default on the part of the first
respondent in completing the project and handing over
possession in terms of the allotment, the buyers are
entitled to delay compensation.
2. In view of the aforesaid allegations made in the affidavit
filed on behalf of home buyers, we deem it appropriate to
require  the  first  respondent  to  file  a  comprehensive
affidavit  disclosing:  (a)  Whether  the  possession  of
completed units of which payments have been received has
been provided to the home buyers mentioned in the list
(Annexure  A  to  the  affidavit);  if  not,  why  delay
compensation be not levied upon the first respondent and
awarded to those home buyers who had made full payment and
had completed the necessary formalities on their part. (b)
Whether the podium, as promised at the time of launching
the project, has been completed or not; if not, why it was
not completed.

matters including contempt petitions. By the next date,

the  been  got  financed  by  the

towards litigation expenses, within a period
of 45 days from the date of receipt of

the said amounts shall carry penal interest
@12% per annum from the date of filing the
complaint till actual realization.”
4. This order came to be challenged by the petitioner before the
National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (‘Commission’). In
para 3 of the impugned order, the Commission records that the
revision was pending since the year 2019. Petitioner did not pursue
the revision petition diligently.
5. On  06.06.2024,  the  following  order  was  passed  by  the
Commission:
“This is a Revision Petition which was on the
mutual consent of the Learned Counsel for the
Petitioner  and  Respondent  No.2  fixed  for
final hearing post 02:00 p.m.
However, when the matter was called at 03:20
p.m.  and  nobody  was  present  for  the
3

## Page 356

Petitioner. 
Much time was wasted in making announcement
both in the Court and around as well as over
the video conference system. Learned Counsel
for  the  Respondent  No.  2  expressed  his
disappointment. 
Apparently,  the  Learned  Counsel  for  the
Petitioner logged off of the video conference
facilities at around 03:25 p.m.
It shows that the Petitioner is not interest
to pursue the matter.
I think this is a fit-case to impose a cost
on the Petitioner. An amount of Rs.5000/-
shall be paid by the Petitioner in the Legal
Aid Fund of this Commission, within six weeks
of this order. Proof of deposit be filed
within eight weeks.
List on 09.12.2024 for final hearing.” 
6. Notwithstanding the same, petitioner continued to default in
pursuing the matter. Consequently, on 15.05.2025, the following
order was passed:
“By  the  Order  dated  06.06.2024,  it  was
mentioned  that  the  Petitioner  is  not
interested to pursue the matter and a cost of
Rs.5,000/-  was  imposed.  Despite  specific
Order for deposit of this amount within six
weeks and proof of deposit to be filed within
eight weeks the same has not been deposited
till dateand the proof of deposit has not
been filed.
This is a Revision Petition of 2019.
Even none appeared for the Petitioner on the
previous date and on 06.06.2024.
4

## Page 357

In view of the aforesaid, we are of the view
that  the  Petitioner  is  not  serious  in
pursuing the matter and the Revision Petition
is dismissed for non-prosecution.” 
7. The Commission, therefore, came to the conclusion that the
petitioner was not diligent enough to prosecute the Revision
Petition. No effort was made to argue the matter. That being the
position, the Commission dismissed the Revision Petition.
8. This order came to be affirmed by the High Court. 
9. We do not find any good reason to interfere in the matter.
10. Consequently, Special Leave Petition is dismissed.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.     OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) No.10054/2026
SATPAL SINGH ALIAS SONI ..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
THE STATE OF JHARKHAND ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. By filing this appeal, appellant has assailed the legality and
correctness of the Order dated 08.04.2026, passed by the High Court
of Jharkhand at Ranchi, (briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter)
rejecting the anticipatory bail application of the appellant.
4. Be it stated that appellant is an accused in B.S. Telco P.S.
Case No.107 of 2023, registered under Sections 341, 342, 323, 324,
307, 384, 379, 364, 504, 506 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860
(for short, ‘IPC’).
5. The accusation against the appellant is that he along with
others forcibly abducted the informant in a vehicle and assaulted
him. The same was done with view to extract ransom. Further
allegation is that appellant had snatched the gold-chain and wallet
1

## Page 379

of the informant.
6. This Court by Order dated 02.06.2026, had issued notice and
granted  interim  protection  to  the  appellant  subject  to  the
appellant cooperating with the investigation and exhibiting good
conduct.
7. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that two of the co-
accused of the appellant have been granted bail; one regular bail
and the other anticipatory bail. Therefore, appellant may be
granted the benefit of anticipatory bail.
8. On the other hand, learned State Counsel submits that there
are three antecedents besides the present one of the appellant. He
is a habitual offender. That apart, in the initial stage he had
evaded the investigation. Therefore, appellant may not be granted
anticipatory bail.
9. Responding  to  the  aforesaid  submission  of  learned  State
Counsel, learned counsel for the appellant submits that out of the
3 antecedents, appellant has been acquitted in one and in the other
two, charge sheets have been filed. In both the matters, appellant
is on bail. He further submits that pursuant to the interim
protection granted by this Court, appellant had appeared before the
Investigating Officer and has cooperated with the investigation.
10. On a query by the Court, learned State counsel submits that
investigation is now complete whereafter charge sheet has been
submitted on 25.07.2026. Matter is now before the Court for framing
of charge.
11. Having regard to to the fact that this Court had granted
interim protection to the appellant while issuing notice pursuant
2

## Page 380

to which he had cooperated with the investigation and the fact that
investigation is complete following which charge sheet has been
filed, we are of the opinion that the interim protection granted to
the appellant may be made absolute.
12. Accordingly, we set aside the impugned order dated 08.04.2026
and make our order dated 02.06.2026 absolute. We direct that
appellant shall appear before the concerned police station once in
every month i.e., on the first Monday of the month at 11:00 am till
commencement of the trial. Once trial commences, he shall render
full cooperation to the trial.
13. Appeal is accordingly disposed of.
14. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.
......................J.
(UJJAL BHUYAN)
......................J.
(ATUL S. CHANDURKAR)
NEW DELHI;
August 12th, 2026.

2. Brief facts necessary to dispose of the present
appeal are, that the appellant was granted a Fair Price
Shop license pursuant to an agreement. Due to a family
dispute,  he  was  arrested  and  released  on  bail  on
16.02.2018.  The agreement was suspended on 30.01.2018,
against  which  he  submitted  a  representation  seeking
revocation  of  the  suspension  of  his  license.
Subsequently,  the  District  Supply  Officer  (for  short,
‘DSO’) cancelled the appellant’s license on the ground
that he had violated Condition No.25 of the agreement.
The said condition stipulated that, in case an allottee
of the license is incarcerated, the license would stands
suspended and upon conviction, it would be cancelled.  A
writ  petition  was  filed  against  the  order  dated
02.04.2018, passed by the D.S.O. by which the Fair Price
1

## Page 391

Shop license of the appellant was cancelled, in view of
the provisions of Clause 4(3) of the U.P. Scheduled
Commodities Distribution Order, 2004 (for short, ‘2004
Order’).  The writ petition preferred by the appellant
was dismissed.
3. Aggrieved by the same, the appellant has challenged
the impugned order dated 05.02.2026 passed by the High
Court of Judicature at Allahabad.  
4. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the
parties.
5. It has been rightly observed by the High Court
itself, that the order dated 02.04.2018 proceeded against
the appellant on the basis of the 2004 Order, which was
subsequently replaced by the U.P. Essential Commodities
(Regulation of Sale and Distribution Control) Order, 2016
(for short, ‘2016 Order’).
6. Despite having rendered the finding that the 2004
Order  will  not  be  applicable  to  the  case  of  the
appellant, the High Court, nonetheless, gave its approval
to the order of the D.S.O., whereby, the license of the
appellant was cancelled, which in our considered view
cannot be sustained in the eyes of law.
7. We  may  also  note  here  that,  certainly,  the
2

## Page 392

respondents  are  entitled  to  take  appropriate  action
against the appellant, in pursuance of the 2016 Order.
8. In such view of the matter, the impugned order dated
05.02.2026, passed by the High Court stands set aside and
consequently, the order dated 02.04.2018 passed by the
D.S.O., also stands set aside.
9. However, liberty is granted to the respondents to
proceed, in accordance with law.
10. Accordingly,  the  appeal  stands  allowed  in  the
aforsesaid terms.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.
………………………………………………………J.
      (M.M. Sundresh)
………………………………………………………J.
       (Prasanna B. Varale)
New Delhi;
August 04, 2026.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NOS.8184-8185/2026
 
UCO BANK               APPELLANT
VERSUS
DEBASHISH NANDA & ANR.             RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. These appeals, challenging the order dated 29 th October,
2025 of the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, New Delhi,
were presented before this Court 5 (five) days beyond the
prescribed period of limitation of 45 (forty-five) days. There was
also a refiling delay of 99 (ninety-nine) days. The delay of 5 (five)
days is not indicated in the office report on limitation being Page A
of the appeal paper book.
2. Though the appellant had applied for condonation of refiling
delay, it did not seek condonation of 5 (five) days’ delay in
presenting the appeals.
3. By an ex  parte  order dated 08 th May, 2026, delay was
condoned by a co-ordinate Bench. Since the appellant had not
applied for condonation of delay in presentation of the appeals
beyond the prescribed period of limitation, such condonation
related to condonation of refiling delay and not to the 5 (five)
days’ delay in presenting the appeals.  
4. Be that as it may, an application has now been filed (I.A.
No.231720/2026) by the respondent no.2, upon service of notice,
seeking recall of the order dated 08 th May, 2026 on the ground
1

## Page 430

that the appeals are time barred and, hence, not maintainable in
the light of the decision of a co-ordinate Bench of this Court in CA
Ramchandra  Dallaram  Choudhary  v.  Adani  Infrastructure
and Developers Private Limited1. 
5. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and learned
senior counsel for the respondent no.2, applicant in I.A.
No.231720/2026. 
6. Having regard to the fact that the appellant did not
represent facts correctly, the order condoning refiling delay is
recalled; also, since the appellant did not seek condonation of 5
(five) days’ delay in presentation of the appeals and refiling delay
beyond 28 (twenty-eight) days cannot be condoned in view of CA
Ramchandra  Dallaram  Choudhary  (supra), the appeals are
dismissed as time-barred. 
7. Interim order, granted earlier, stands vacated forthwith.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

2. The  present  Special  Leave  Petition  calls  in
question the correctness of the order dated 19 th March,
2026 passed by the High Court at Calcutta in the Circuit
Bench at Jalpaiguri in CRM (R) No. 09 of 2026 whereby the
High Court has rejected the bail application of the
petitioner in connection with FIR No.1094 of 2025 dated
6th November,  2025  registered  at  Police  Station
Bhaktinagar,  District  Jalpaiguri,  Calcutta  for  the
offences punishable under Sections 64, 123 and 351(2) of
the Bharatiya Nyaya Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.
3. Being aggrieved, the petitioner filed the present
petition seeking bail.  When the matter came up on 8 th
May, 2026,  this Court passed the following order and
enlarged the petitioner on interim bail:
“1. The notice issued to the Respondent No.2
(original complainant) has not yet been served. 
2. In the facts and circumstances of this case,
we order that the petitioner who is in judicial
custody since 6th November 2025 be released on
interim bail, subject to terms and conditions
that the trial court may deem fit to impose.
3. We shall proceed to pass the final order after
hearing the Respondent No.2 after two weeks.”
4. Respondent No.2, though served, has chosen not to
appear.

parties and perused the records.

of the case, we confirm the order dated 8 th May, 2026.

terms and conditions, pending trial.

above terms.

O R D E R
1. Delay condoned. 
2. Leave granted. 
3. The appellants are aggrieved by the dismissal of their quash
petition in Criminal Miscellaneous No. 57171/2017, vide order
dated 12.12.2023 passed by the High Court of Judicature at
Patna.
4. Perusal of the said order reflects that the only reason that
weighed with the High Court in doing so was the submission
made before it to the effect that the trial had already
commenced and seven witnesses had been examined. 
5. While so, the learned counsel for the State of Bihar fairly
concedes that the aforesaid averment made before the High
Court was incorrect, as the trial had not even commenced by
the date the High Court passed the impugned order. 
6. As the matter was disposed of by the High Court on a
1

## Page 448

misconception  of  the  factual  position,  the  order  under
challenge cannot be sustained and is, accordingly, set aside.
In consequence, Criminal Miscellaneous No. 57171/2017 shall
stand restored to the file of the High Court. 
7. The matter shall be considered on its own merits and in
accordance with law as expeditiously as possible, keeping in
mind the length of time that has elapsed owing to the earlier
order being passed on a mistaken impression on facts. 
8. The appeal is, accordingly, allowed in the aforestated terms. 
9. Pending applications, if any, shall stand disposed of.

CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.       OF 2026
(arising out of SLP(CRL.) No. 12606/2025)
C.R. RAMBABU ..... APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE REPRESENTED BY THE 
INSPECTOR OF POLICE
..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1.  Leave granted.
2. The appellant, C.R. Rambabu, is aggrieved by the condition
imposed by the High Court of Judicature at Madras, vide order
dated 15.07.2024 in Criminal Original Petition No. 15214/2024,
that he should deposit a sum of 15,00,000/- (Rupees fifteen₹
lakhs only) to avail the benefit of interim anticipatory bail
in relation to First Information Report (FIR) No. 45/2024
registered with Police Station – Avadi, District – Avadi City
CCB, for the offences punishable under Sections 408, 409 and
420  of  the  Indian  Penal  Code,  1860.  Thereafter,  his
application for modification of the condition was dismissed.
3. By order dated 13.08.2025, this Court stayed the aforestated
condition. 
4. Having heard the learned counsel for the parties and in view
of the various judgments passed by this Court holding that
criminal proceedings cannot be used as a means of recovery,
1

## Page 466

whereby conditions can be imposed with regard to deposit of
monies so as to avail the benefit of regular bail/anticipatory
bail, we are of the opinion that the High Court was not
justified in imposing such a condition in the facts of the
present case. It is only in exceptional circumstances that the
Court would be justified in imposing such a condition and we
find  no  such  exceptional  ground  having  been  made  out
presently. 
5. The  appeal  is,  accordingly,  allowed,  setting  aside  the
condition imposed by the High Court that the appellant should
deposit the sum of 15,00,000/- (Rupees fifteen lakhs only) as₹
a condition precedent for availing the benefit of anticipatory
bail. The appellant is entitled to the benefit of the order of
anticipatory bail, independent thereof. 
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of. 
.....................J.
(SANJAY KUMAR)
.....................J.
(SANJEEV SACHDEVA)
NEW DELHI;
JULY 14, 2026.

2. We  are  not  inclined  to  interfere  with  the  impugned
judgment/order(s) passed by the High Court, refusing to call

## Page 478

2
for the records pertaining to chargesheet and quash the same.
3. However, we grant liberty to the petitioners to avail any
other  statutory  remedy  that  may  be  available  to  the
petitioners including the application for discharge on all
grounds  that  are  available  to  the  petitioners.  If  such
discharge applications are moved, that may be decided on their
own merits uninfluenced by any of the observations of the High
Court’s order or by this Court’s order.
4. At  this  stage,  learned  Senior  Counsel  for  the
petitioners, drawing attention to the judgment of the High
Court dated 07.08.2019 in the case of the petitioners, when
they sought to quash the FIR, and submitted that the detailed
observations  made  therein  will  come  in  the  way  of  the
petitioners.
5. We have perused the said judgment dated 07.08.2019. That
judgment arose in the context of a prayer for quashment of FIR
before the chargesheet was filed. We have also noticed from
the  said  judgment,  the  following  observations  carefully
engrafted by the learned Single Judge of the High Court in
paragraph 33-
”……...The  Court  should  not  put  spokes  in  the
investigation  and  should  necessarily  allow  the
respondent police to complete the investigation.  Only
on  the  completion  of  the  investigation,  a  clear
picture will emerge and the purpose for which such a
huge  consignment  was  brought  in,  will  stand
established.”
(emphasis supplied)

## Page 479

3
6. These observations will make it clear that whatever was
said in the judgment dated 07.08.2019 was for the purpose of
declining quashment of proceedings at the FIR stage. Today,
the chargesheet has been filed after investigation.
7. We make it clear that the application for discharge,
which the petitioners propose to file, will be decided keeping
in mind the observations of the learned Single Judge in
paragraph 33 of the judgment dated 07.08.2019.
8. Parties are granted liberty to raise all contentions.
9. All contentions are left open to be decided independently
and on their own merits. 
10. With these observations, the Special Leave Petition is
disposed of.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NOS. 12694 - 12695 OF 2025
AMAR NATH & ORS.  ...APPELLANTS
versus
SHRI SATPAL & ORS. ...RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. The short question that arises for our consideration
in these appeals is as to whether the High Court of Punjab
and Haryana at Chandigarh was right in remitting the matter
to the learned Trial Court for reconsideration  vide the
impugned order. 
2. This Court, by its order dated 11.08.2025, expressed
a prima facie  view, relevant portion thereof, which reads
as under:
“Prima facie, we are inclined to set aside the
impugned order and remit the matter to the High
Court, and request the High Court to decide the
matter after getting a finding from the Trial
Court with respect to the share of all the
respondents.
.. .. .. .. .. .. ..”
4. On a perusal of the impugned order, we find that while
answering the substantial question of law and assigning
reasons, the High Court was pleased to set aside the
judgment of the First Appellate Court by remitting the
1

## Page 490

matter to the concerned Trial Court.
5. We hold that such an approach is impermissible in the
eye of law.
6. In such view of the matter, we set aside the impugned
order and remit the matter to the High Court for fresh
consideration.  All the issues are left open, including the
issue of maintainability, for which, the High Court can
frame a substantial question of law, if not done already
and, thereafter, present it to the parties to answer the
same.
7. Furthermore, keeping in view the long pendency of the
suit, we request the High Court to make an endeavour to
expeditiously  dispose  of  the  matter  being  remitted,
preferably within a period of six months from today.
8. Accordingly, the appeals stand disposed of.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.
………………………………………………………J.
   (M.M. SUNDRESH)
………………………………………………………J.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. It was claimed by the appellant, viz. A. G. Udayasankar in paragraphs 1 &
2 of the writ petition 1 instituted by him before the High Court of Kerala at
Ernakulam that he was promoted as an Executive Engineer on 11 th September,
2001 under the 7-tier system; however he was not given the benefit of such
promotion by fixing his pay and allowance.
2. Our attention has been drawn to an order dated 30th January, 2009 passed
1 W.P. (C) No.2251/2005
1

## Page 511

on such writ petition by a learned Judge of the High Court to the effect that the
principle  settled  by  the  Division  Bench  of  the  High  Court  in  Writ  Appeal
Nos.2503/2005 and 2462/2005 would govern the case of the appellant.
3. Writ Appeal Nos.2503/2005 and 2462/2005 were appeals by the State of
Kerala challenging the orders passed by the Single Judge granting relief to
engineers similarly placed as the appellant. Such appeals were dismissed by the
Division Bench on 11th January, 2010 holding that those who have worked in the
promoted post till their dates of retirement would be entitled to salary on the
promoted post and that such engineers do have the legal right to claim the
benefit.
4. If indeed the claim of the appellant that he was similarly circumstanced as
the engineers who succeeded before the Division Bench is correct, he should
have been held entitled to the same benefits which were extended to the other
engineers by in the other round of proceedings. However, what we find is that
though the appellant succeeded before the Single Bench, a Division Bench
allowed the intra-court appeal of the State of Kerala and reversed the decision
allowing the writ petition.   
5. Since the order of promotion of the appellant is not on record, we grant
him seven days’ time to file an application for additional documents to bring the
same on record.
6. At the same time, we require the State to substantiate the statement
made by it in paragraph 10 of its memorandum of appeal giving rise to Writ
Appeal No.904/2012 to the effect that the appellant was promoted under the
normal course of promotion from the post of Assistant Executive Engineer to
Executive Engineer as per order dated 06th September, 2011.
7.  Similar  liberty  is  granted  to  the  other  appellant  viz.  in  C.  J.
Chandrasekharan in Civil Appeal No.9382/2016.
2

## Page 512

8. The appeals are heard in part.
9. Relist the appeals after six weeks.

attention of this Court to the Interlocutory Application No.195057
of 2026 and submits that despite the Unit/Rice and Flour Mill being
sealed by the Police, in connivance with the Police, the respondent
no.1 has removed the bulk of the plant and machinery from the said
Mill, which are of substantial value.
3. Having regard to the aforesaid, let the respondent no.2-State
of Maharashtra file an affidavit in response to the averments made
in the said Interlocutory Application No.195057 of 2026.
4. The Commissioner of Police, Nagpur, Maharashtra, shall conduct
a personal inquiry into the matter as his/her own Police Force is
alleged to be in connivance with the respondent no.1. A report
would be submitted as to whether after the premises was locked by
the Police, the same was opened and the respondent no.1 was allowed
to remove the plant and the machinery from the premises, which was

## Page 530

sealed. The report shall also cover as to whether any attempt has
been made by the respondent no.1 to siphon off any assets acquired
by him.
5. We  indicate  that  if  there  is  any  indication  of  their
connivance or the report of the Commissioner, Nagpur, Maharashtra,
is not objective, fair and without any extraneous consideration,
the Court would come down heavily on the authorities concerned
especially the person submitting the report i.e., the Commissioner
of  Police,  Nagpur,  Maharashtra.  The  said  affidavit  shall  be
personally  affirmed  by  the  Commissioner  of  Police,  Nagpur,
Maharashtra and submitted within three weeks.

part-heard.

## Page 535

2. Despite valid service of notice, nobody has appeared on
behalf of the respondent no.2.
3. The petitioner seeks anticipatory bail in connection
with G.D.  No.046 of 2024 in FIR No.301 dated 12.11.2024,
registered at Police Station Phillaur, District Jalandhar
Rural, Punjab under Sections 117(2), 118(2), 191(3) and 190
of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
4. The allegation specifically against the petitioner is
that he had injured one Nakshu on the head by stone.
5. Vide  order dated 10.08.2026, we had asked the learned
counsel for the respondent no.1-State of Punjab to produce
the medical report of the said Nakshu and today, the same has
been brought on record.
6. The said report indicates that there is a lacerated
wound in the middle part of biparietal region of the skull
near vertex.
7. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that there
was a case and a counter case and both the sides were injured
and in the present case, only mild lacerated injury has been
caused though from the FIR, it sounds to be very serious. It
was further contended that the Doctor had opined that the
injury was simple in nature. Further, it was submitted that
the petitioner has no criminal antecedent.

## Page 536

3
8. Learned counsel for the respondent no.1-State of Punjab
submits that though there was a fight between two groups and
there is a counter case, but the petitioner had also played
an active overt role.
9. Having considered the matter in its entirety and the
fact that there is a counter case in which, the petitioner
side has also been injured and the injury attributed to the
petitioner is simple in nature, being a lacerated wound and
there is no criminal antecedent, we are persuaded to allow
the prayer for grant of anticipatory bail to the petitioner.
10. Accordingly, in the event of arrest or surrender within
two weeks from today, the petitioner shall be released on
bail, subject to his cooperation in the investigation/trial.
11. The Special Leave Petition stands disposed of in the
aforementioned terms.
12. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  also  stand
disposed of.

              VERSUS
STATE OF BIHAR ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. Appellant’s prayer for bail has been rejected by the High
Court of Judicature at Patna (briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter)
by way of the impugned order dated 17.10.2023.
4. Allegation against the appellant is under Sections 394/302 of
the Indian Penal Code, 1860  (for short, ‘IPC’). As per the
prosecution case, wife of the informant was killed by criminals
when they broke into their house and looted 1,50,000/- and other₹
valuable articles.
5. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that appellant is in
custody since 07.02.2023, which is more than 3 years and 7 months.
He has referred to the counter affidavit filed by the respondent-
State, more particularly to paragraph 26 thereof, and submits that
appellant does not have any criminal antecedents. Narrating the
events leading to registration of the First Information Report,
learned counsel submits that it is a case of blind murder and
nothing incriminating against the appellant has come out thus far.
1

## Page 556

Therefore, appellant may be enlarged on bail.
6. Learned State counsel on the other hand has taken us to
paragraph 20 of the counter affidavit and submits that only 3
witnesses remained to be examined; 2 doctors and the investigating
officer.
7. While we are conscious of the fact that appellant is in
custody for more than 3 and a half years, we find that substantial
progress has been made in the trial. We are of the view that the
trial would be over within a maximum period of 6 weeks from today.
If  the  trial  is  not  concluded  within  the  aforesaid  period,
appellant would be at liberty to renew his prayer for bail before
this Court.
8. For the moment, we are not inclined to enlarge the appellant
on bail.
9.  Consequently, the appeal is disposed of.
10. Pending applications, if any, shall also stand disposed of.

3. It has been stated that the petitioner-wife is the
sole earning member of her family and she is looking
after her elderly parents and it is very difficult for
her to travel all alone.
4. This  Court  after  taking  into  consideration  the
grounds raised by the petitioner and also keeping in
view the fact that there is no appearance on behalf of
the respondent-husband,  this Court is of the opinion
that  the  present  transfer  petition  deserves  to  be
allowed.

O R D E R
1. Learned counsel appearing for the appellants has been heard.
2. Respondents are not called upon to answer.
3. The judgment and order dated 21 st November, 2012 of the High Court of
Kerala at Ernakulam dismissing the appellants’ writ petition 1 under Article 226
of the Constitution is under challenge. Interpreting Rule 13AA and Rule 13AB of
the Kerala State and Subordinate Service Rules, 1958 correctly, the High Court
has held that SC/ST entrants in service beyond 31st December, 1985 are obliged
to qualify in the special test and since the appellants failed to so qualify, they
were rightly reverted from the posts of Upper Division Clerk to Lower Division
Clerk. 
4. We see no reason to interfere with the impugned judgment and order;
hence, the civil appeal is dismissed.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following

1. Having heard learned counsel appearing for the parties, we notice that the
present petition is directed against the interim order dated 30.06.2025
1

## Page 711

whereunder notice has been issue to respondent(s) therein, namely, the
petitioner(s) herein and the FIR registered against the respondent(s) herein had
been stayed.
2.  Being  aggrieved  by  the  same  the  petitioner-wife  (complainant)  has
approached this Court in the present petition. Having regard to the relationship
between the parties, the dispute was referred to Supreme Court Mediation
Centre vide order dated 09.01.2026 and under the said order we had also
directed that no coercive steps shall be taken against Respondent Nos.1 to 3
during  pendency of the present petition.
3. Having regard to the fact that issue is still at large before the High Court, we
deem it appropriate to request the High Court to expedite hearing and the order
passed that no coercive steps be taken against the respondents herein shall
continue till disposal of the petition by the High Court. 
4. We dispose of this petition, by requesting the High Court to dispose of the
petition filed by respondent Nos. 1 to 3 herein under Section 482 CrPC
expeditiously and during the pendency of the said petition no coercive steps
shall be taken against the Respondent Nos. 1 to 3. However, we make it clear
that, investigation, if any, has been concluded, the final report shall be placed
before the jurisdictional Court after bringing it to the notice of the High Court.
5.  Accordingly,  the  Special  Leave  Petition  stands  disposed  of.  Pending
application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

         UPON hearing the counsel, the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
We are not inclined to interfere with the impugned order
passed by the Madras High Court granting anticipatory bail to
respondent No. 1, in the light of the fact that the Inspector of
Police, E-1, Ponneri Police Station, Redhills District, Chennai,
1

## Page 891

SLP(Crl.) No. 9809/2026
Tamil  Nadu,  filed  a  status  report,  wherein  he  stated  that
respondent No. 1 has joined the investigation and is presently
cooperating.
However, we may note that the High Court was not justified in
making an observation in paragraph 6 of the impugned order to the
effect  that  the  dispute  was  civil  in  nature,  as  criminal
proceedings had already been initiated and were in progress.
The trial Court shall not be influenced by the aforestated
observation made by the High Court.
We may also note that, in the status report, the Inspector of
Police stated that the investigation was at an advanced stage and
nearing completion.  
As  the  First  Information  Report  in  question  is  dated
24.09.2025, the State shall endeavour to file its final report as
expeditiously as possible.
Subject to the above observations, the special leave petition
is dismissed.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

1. After hearing the arguments and upon finding that the
matter was concluded by concurrent findings of fact
returned by the Trial Court and the High Court on the
existence of agreement; readiness and willingness and
other issues, we had indicated in order dated 31.07.2026
that we do not propose to entertain this special leave
1

## Page 1063

petition on merit.  However, on equity, to ensure that
the petitioner(s) are able to get some value for the
constructions made over the land during the pendency of
the  proceedings,  we  had  requested  the  respondent(s)
counsel  to  explore  whether  the  decree  needs  to  be
modified to suitably compensate the petitioner(s) for the
amounts spent by them.
2. The learned counsel for the respondent(s) had offered
Rs.20 lakhs for the constructions standing on the land,
without prejudice to the rights of the respondent(s).
However  that  offer  is  not  acceptable  to  the
petitioner(s).  
3. It may be placed on record that the constructions raised
by the petitioner(s) were during the pendency of the
proceedings and permitted without prejudice to the rights
of the parties.  In such circumstances, we are of the
view that the petitioner(s) are not entitled to seek any
equity on basis of such constructions.  
4. As the petitioner(s) are not willing to accept the offer
made by the respondent(s), we have no option but to
dismiss the special leave petition.
5. The special leave petition is, accordingly, dismissed.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
